concurrently in disciplining the thought and
conduct of the working men of the towns will
lead to an action on the part of the workers of

England over the whole field of labour, which
will have a very decided influence for the

_
better on the condition of the working classes

generally.
The artizan class in our larger and most
important industries have taken their first
steps—they have joined themselves together
for mutual aid, and have taken to definitions
of their rights, and discussions of their inte-

rests. From these discussions and definitions
have come the oft zopeated and generally
believed statement—that the great question
of the day is the "labour question." Mr.
CARLYLE put this before the country years
ago, but he put it more as a puzzling, sadden-
ing, almost inexplicable problem than as a
question of definite shape, with intelligible,
understood, but deferred issues. "The great
labour question" is not in this position now.
It is daily becoming less encumbered by the
mistakes and confusions of prejudice, ignor-
ance, and a blind self-interest. Increase bf
trade without a corresponding increase in
men, coupled with a marked advance in the
spirit and practice of union amongst the
workers are gradually altering the relative
positions of labour and capital, and bringing
about conditions of co-operation in action
which a few years back would have been
regarded as impossible.
The observant reader may pick up from odd
paragraphs in the corners of our newspapers
facts which throw a strong light into the
future, and enable us to see with some degree
of distinctness the probable condition of the
things towards which we are advancing. It
is not necessary to be prejudiced either for
or
.against emigration to watch the outflowing
stream and speculate on the probable effect of
such a continued and continuously increasing
exodus of labour. To save the pressure on the

poor rates numbers of the most indigent are
sent out of the country by publio subscription.
To protect themselves from the anxieties of
constantly recurring periods of distress in-
dustrious working men flee the land of their
birth, whilst uncertainty as to the future

fate of children drives many an affectionate
father across the Atlantic to find safer homes
for those from whom death may any moment
separate him. Emigration has done its work
pretty fairly in Ireland. It is now increasing
very rapidly in England. lathe Daily News
a few days since appeared the following :
"The Exodus from Liverpool this year has
commenced with unparalleled dimensions. In
fact, the vast increase in emigration during
the month of April has never before been
equalled. Notwithstanding the great number
of emigrants who leave the different
Irish ports for Canada and the United
States, of steerage passengers alone to
these two places 11,606 persons went from ,
England—figures which, taken as repre-
senting one month, really show an almost
alarming increase in English emigration.
We are not informed whether these persons
come from the agricultural districts or from
the towns, but, wherever they were furnished
from, the effect on the labour market will be
very striking and very decided. If they have
gone from the towns, they will have left room
for others to pass from the fields into their
places, and if they have gone for the most
part directly from the fields, then we may
regard ourselves as at the beginning of a move-

ment as remarkable in its way as that

wonderful exodus which drained off the

starving population of Ireland a few years
since.

During this time our industry must go on
increasing, factories will be built and work-
shops erected, and though no doubt the
periodical panic will come, as far as the
workers are concerned, it will drive them
but the more rapidly out of the country—and
we shall be left, on a new revival of trade, with
a still larger demand for labour than we have
at present, and far less ability
,to supply it
than we now possess.
In the meantime, the immediate work to be
done is to perfect the unions in the agricultural
districts. Every village, every hamlet, should
be the centre of a union. There should be no
half-doing, and there is no need—with the
experience possessed by the trades societies at
hand—for imperfect doing. There should be
no violence, nor any approach even towards it.
Let our labourers trust in themselves, to their
English rights, to the laws under which they
live, and to their fellow workers in the town,
who will aid them in every legitimate way.
They should bear in mind that any body who
seeks to excite disturbance or breach of the
peace is an enemy, and as such he should
not be listened to.

Let the laws of your own land,
Good or ill, between you stand,
Hand to hand and foot to liot,

Arbiters of the dispute.

The right of union is not now denied; the
power of union will be thus secured. Our
labourers will stand together and move
altogether; the will of all will be as the will
of one; and. the demands decided on and
made with unanimity must in the very nature
of things be conceded.
It has been said already that the present
demands of the labourers; moderate as they
are, must ruin the farmer. And it is suggested
that future demands originating in a con-
sciousness of newly-acquired strength must
most inevitably lead to a great social
revolution. With this at the present stage
of the proceedings the agricultural labourers
have little or nothing to do. The formation of
unions and the advancement of wages are the
questions and the only questions to be con-
sidered. Questions of rents, leases, prices of
produce, game laws, character of original
ownership may, so far as they are concerned, be
allowed to go to sleep for a time. Many of
these are of the very highest importance and
will have to be dealt with vigorously and in
time. The country generally will have
to deal with them; the legislature
will have to take them in hand. Farmers
and landlords will be compelled. to bestir them-
selves in regard to them. But the labourers,
if they are wise, will allow others to deal with
these, and meddle only with their unions and
their wages. One fact they must, by insisting
on, keep before the eyes of the world as not
to be tolerated, not to be put aside, which is,
that the life of the field-worker is no longer
endurable on twelve shillings a week. They
must say determinedly that if it be a question
between the continuance of a condition of
things so intolerable and the ruin of England,
that the ruin of England must be risked in
the attempt to improve it. If the farmer gets
shaken because he has not capital enough, if
the landlord. gets uncomfortable because be
has paid a very high price for his land, and if
other people get uncomfortable for a multitude

PRICE ONE

of reasons not worth naming, it cannot IA
helped; all this must happen rather than the
labourer shall go on working at twelve shillings
a week. It is true that many people will regard.
mere union and advance of wages as mean
and petty things to fight for in the presence of
so many things that obstruct our passage in
the direction of the millennium. But it
must not be forgotten they are those in which
the labourer is most dirbctly interested, and
for which he Will fightwith most determination.
It may be added, tob, that philauthrophists
and philosophers heed not grumble at this,
inasmuch as these questions carry in them all
' the others. If by lifting the foundation we
put out of gear the joints and bindings of the
structure, we shall simply have to do our best
to rearrange them and make them, if possible,
stronger than before.
This movement of the agricultural labourers
is, rightly looked at, the most hopeful move-
ment which has taken place for centuries in
England; and it is doubly hopeful by the
character of the men who have been put to
the front. The advice and aid of the com-
bined men of the towns actively and
decisively given, is w hat is now most needed.
Everything will be said by the press
and by exalted "labourers friends" to
prevent this, but clear-sighted, intelligent
men will disregard such talk and do their duty.
Our great trades unions are the "big brothers;
they have strength and pluck, discipline,
arms, experience, everything that can tend to
promote victory, and their friendly disposition
should not NI short of the requirements of
the situation. Every proper agency must be
set in motion io bring the help of the towns-
man to his rur,il brother. We have now got
at the root, there is a quickening there, a new
vitality full of promise for the future, and no
higher crime afrYainst the catHe of labour can be
committed than to withhold anything necessary
to secure its healthy, direet, and vigorous
action.

LLOYD JONES.

THE LAND QUESTION AND THE AGRI-
CULTURAL LABOURERS.
Tun laud question, which was looming in
the distance, has been brought to the front, by
an agency long believed to be too contemptible
for notice. If anything proves how the preda-
tory instinct of mankind will indulge itseli iii
preying upon its fellow-men whenever there
is impunity for its voracity, and think itself
right in doing so, the practice of the land-
owners and fatmers—men not natui ally bad—
upon the poor cultivators of the si il, the agri-
cultural labourers, affords that proof in a pre-
eminent degree of atrocity. All the while
these landlords and farmers, from the absence
of complaints from the labourers, and, therefore,
believing in their complete impunity, carrying
their heads high in the belief of their unim-
peachable kindness and morality, never for a
moment thinking of what they were doing
while they were inflicting worse than negro
slavery On these unfortunate labourers. And
that, too, in the undoubted. belief that it was
the duty of these. white slaves to toil, to starve,
and, besides toiling and starving as adults, to
be subject in their youth, both male and.
female, to demoralization worse than that of
savage life ; in order that they, the landlords
and farmers, might lima to the extent of so
many pounds a year, at time expense, the
slavery of the bodies, and the imminence of
perdition t.'J the souls,
.uf these. youthful

MOVEMENT AMONGST AGRICULTURAL
LABOURERS.
Tan Agricultural Labour Conference, held
last week at Willis's Rooms, had several
features of interest which should not be over-
looked. For the first time, it may be said,
the actual labourer in the flesh—the man who
digs, and ploughs, and sows, and reaps—he
who has been the subject of " commission "
enquiries, without being thoroughly found
out—he whom Mr. DisnA.ELI assures us
everybody is so ignorant about, who seems to
change shape and become something else even
whilst we look at him—
" The moment that you had pronounced him one,
Presto! his face changed, and ho was another."
This man put in an appearance himself, and
as it were, taking the word out of tho mouths
of country gentlemen, newspaper writers, and
others, told his own tale; how he works, how
much he gets, and what he suffers. Not only
did he do this, but he did it well, in a manly,
clear, and intelligent manner; in plain, simple,
honest, eloquent, earnest words. Nothing
could be better than the way in which Mr.
Amu and his brother delegates stated their
case. There was no anger or exaggeration in
their words, no abuse of the farmer or the
landlord. In fact the impression derived from
their statements was that they themselves are
sound and sensible, that their case is a
thoroughly good one, and that whether they
succeeded or not they certainly deserve to
do so.

• It is a misfortune, however, that at such
meetings as those held at Willis's Rooms, there
is a great difficulty in getting at the true
question to be discussed and sticking to it
when it is laid hold of. No blame attaches to
the agricultural delegates on this head. They
knew perfectly that their first consideration
was how to put themselves into union and
remain in it. They seemed struck with the
fact that the anger of their employers is
directed more strongly against their disposition
to maintain their unions than it is against the
demand Made for increased wages. This,
however, is
...precisely the experience of all
working men who have travelled the path
upon which they have just entered; and their
visit to London will enable them to under-
stand this in the right way. Their conviction
that an increase of wages was a necessity,
needed no strengthening. Upon that point
there could be no divided opininion, nor was
there, as even the stoutest -,stickler for the
farmer admitted that something ough tto be done
to improve the condition of the labourer.
That these two preliminary questions will lead
up to others there can be no doubt. Four or
five years of organising strength will give
these men a power they have not the least
idea of at present. And the sale time spent

labourers promiscuously herded together, male
and female, in what they were pleased to term
agricultural gangs.
Nor does this •Admit of the least dispute.
The parliamentary evidepee on the state of
the agricultural labourers and the agricultural
gangs, prove this beyond all question.

The -Rev. Canon GIRDLESToNE, so long ago
as March 28th, 1868, at a meeting in Willis's
Rooms, and afterwards at the British Associa-
tion for the Promotion of Social Science,
brought their abject awl most deplorable con-
dition before the public; without, at the
time, much effeot. At the British Social
Science meeting, August 21st, 1868, his paper,
exposing their true condition was met by the
" sarans " of that Society, with Professor
LtoNn Livr at their head—great as usual in

ments, though these statements, were, indis-
putably true, and well-known to be so; simply

the greatest possible" toadies" to the rich; and
the exposure Of
,their miseries at that time
came to neihing. But "God helps them who
help themselves." The agriciatural labourers
have now lkgun to help.themselves by form-
ing themsel yes into Trades' Unions, and it must
be acknowledged that they have met with
cotinte wince, cncourageinent, and support.
Firit hem the trade's unionists of the towns,
the ;thudganiated engineers taking the lead, in
the p,.; son of Mr. ALLAN, their secretary, fol-
lowed naly by :other Trade's' Unions; and
almost simultaneously from gentlemen who
favoured that mode of the toilers asserting their
independence; and then from certain. land-
lords,pr. SEELEY for instance, who practically
set the example of remedying the evil, by
enteritig. into an agreement with his. tenant
farniers to reduce their rents where needful,
to allow of proper wages being paid to the
Onitivators of the soil; and, lastly, the move-
ment has been acknowledged by the Haus° of
Corranons by a discussion on the Land Question,
introduced, April 9th, by Mr. FOWLER, in
Consequence of the agricultural strikes; and
by a discussion in
,the same House on the
franchise, as applicable to the agricultural
labourers, which, it is true, resulted in a
minority of 78 against pledging the House at
present to grant it. But a minority number-
ing 78 in a House of 148 on such a subject
from such a clinic; is an immense prpgress, in
,
so short a time, in its favour.
AU this has resulted from the circumstance of
they agrieultural labourers " helping them-
selves," by fortning themselves into trades
unions. Nothing could be done without this
most indispensable condition. At a meeting
called by the Rev. Canon GIRDLESTONZ at
Willis's Rooms, above referred to, March 28th.
1868, a most influential assembly was co n'Vened
consisting of Members of both Houses of Par-
liament, of independent gentlemen, and of
representative men of the working classes.
To this meeting the state of the agricultural
labourers was depicted by the Rev. CANON in
terms which are now familiar to all the reiders
of newspapers. But, although the formation
of the labourers into trades unions was one of
the remedies pointed out by the Rev. CANON,
there Wilki no sign, or the hope of any signs of
movement ,by themselves; indeed, as far as
could understand, the hope seemed to be, that
that .meeting might perhaps point out how
trades unions might, be formed among them,
which of course was not possible. Such
movements, in attempt at least, must always
come from the parties themselves. The late
Mr. O'CoNNELL's oft-repeated quotation,
" Hereditary bondsmen, know ye not,
Would you be free, yourselves must strike the
blow,"
is most true in all cases of this kind. In vain
did Mr. PAWdftT, ALP., and certain noble
lords and gentlemen, make suggestions and
discuss the matter pro and con, and that too,
with good diacretion. The movement at that
time came to nothing. About the best thing,
and certainly the truest, that was said there,
was by !Ali. GEORGE PorrEti.of the BEE;•HIVE,
who pointed out "that if the noble lords and
gentlemen who owned the laud eared as much
for the agricultural labourers, whe tilled their

soil, as they did for their dogs and horses, the
state of these labourers would be very differ-
ent." This was too true not to moot with a
burst of indignant denial from that Meet
ing—which was "very respectable "—but
which, notwithstanding, everybody then
present, in his heart of hearts thoroughly
believed. But, although nothing immediately
resulted, the seed was sown at this meeting,
which is new bearing fruit. Some of the
results of this fruit were shown at a similar,.
but more recent meeting (April 30, 1872), in
the same place, Willis's Rooms, in which the
Rev. CoN and some of the same parties who
took part in the meeting of March, 1868, were
present, assisted by others, who were now
actually engaged in carrying out these agricul-
tural unions. (See Daily Telegraph, May 1,
1872, and the BE.E..flivE Of last week.)
The philosophy of the subject is very simple.
There are three °lasses who derive revenue.
from the-produce of the land. The landlords,
the farmers, and the actual cultivators of the
soil, the agricultural labourers. The. lion's
share has hitherto, been monopolised. by the
landlords and farmers, while the labourers
have been reduced to. mere starvation wages,
This will now be altered, but to make such
alteration permanent there must be permanent
diminution in the number of labourers, either
by emigration, or by i 'lessening of. their
natural increase. But there is another way
by which, for O. considerable]. tithe, 'higher,
wages may be paid,, namely by such alterations
in the laws of Primogeniture and Entail, as
shall lessen or do away with "life ownership"
In the land, which =lwo it to a certain ex-
tent practically sterile.. In the meantime,
however, trades unions among the agricultural
laboirers will improve their condition, and
more than anything else, will indirectly tend
to alter, or to cause the repeal of these most
pernicious laws.
. This is, however, too extensive a subject to
enter upon how. While these laws exist, and
Under which the number of labourers have
increased above the number required for the
cultivation of the soil, nothing permanently
effectual as a remedy for the poverty of the
agricultural labourers can take place, for the
, same cause will continually produce the same
effect. Where these laws 'do not exist, as in
France and elsewhere, and the existence of
peasant proprietors is an accomplished fact,
there is no over supply of population or over
likely to be; and, consequently, the greatest
source of "vice and misery" there has no
existence. There may be no sign of super-
abundant riches, but there is no squalor and
no misery.

To produce that change here must be a
work of time, and the change is and must be
gradual. But there is no reason why it should
not take plaeo. These pernicious laws being
repealed, the required change would take
place by the mere effluxion of time, without
injury to anyone. And from what has taken
place in this country, I am inclined to think
that such a change brought about in this
way, without political convulsion, is quite
possible. _ _

IN your impression of the 4th inst. appears
a short letter, signed G. W. FIELD, criticising
the above publication. Your. correspondent
says,--:" All writing for the people• should be
short, sharp, clear, and cheap." , This is. very
true, but the questions to be handled are so
various, and the interests so numerous and
complex, that it would be impossible to do
justice to so important a subject in shorter
space. The author must have bestowed upon
it a life-long study, and deserves the thanks
of his country for the labour of love (which it
certainly is)
,that has produced such a collec-
tion of facts and figures. As to the cheapness,
where is there a new book of nearly a thousand
pages to be bought for the price, is. ad. ?
Why, as you remark in your review, the paper
and printing must have cost the money, and
were it not that he is comparatively a rich
man, he must have felt the loss keenly that
the issue of this book at the price has brought
him. I quite agree with Arr. FIELD that
7s. Gd. is a great deal for a working man to
pay for one book, but I would recommend
AIL FIELD lila feiV others of the no4e,lled

working men's friends to buy a number of
copies, and issue thein to the working men's
clubs and institutions, where they can
be seen at intervals by each in their
turn, or some of the most, vital pages
selebted for a sort of penny reading on
a certain evening each, week, where all could '
listen and discussion invited. I have bought
soorna copies with this view, and am.ready
to make a contribution to any of these institu-
tions on application.
But Mr. Field may after all be one of those
half
,and half free traders who cannot see
their way clear, to abolish taxes on luxuries
for fear of making beer and tobacco come too
cheap to the working man, and thereby tempt
him into the gin shop. .Or perhaps he is of
the opinion of some, of our M.P.'s who, pro-
fesing to be the working man's friend, can
write to me in the following strain, after
reading my papers on Free Trade
"MY DEAR have read your letter and
the inclosures, I have nothing to say against
...our principles. lan as strong a free trader as
you are, though not in favour of the complete aboli-
tion of indirect taxation,. which is, the. only,.or at
least the least felt, method of getting the poor to
- bear their share of the public burthens.

Now I think 99 out of every 100 working
men will be sure t 9 see the cloven foot peep-
ing out of the words I have italicised. If in-
direct taxation had no worse tendency than
getting the working classes to pay "their
fair share of the public burdens, there would
be little to say against Such line of argument ;
but I know from experience that this Blue Book
proves the 'truth to be tbat they have a far
different tendency, they tend to make the
working men pay enormously more than his
fair share, besides making them suffer priva-
tions incidental to the want of honest and
profitable employment.
_ _ _

If Mr. FIELD be sincere in his observations
about making the writing for the millions.
short, sharp, clear, and cheap, let me suggest
that he select a few paragraphs from the Blue
Book, and I am sure you and a few other
editors will print them in your cheap penny
papers.

For instance, ho might point out what occurs

in pages 362 and 363 to the effect that, Such
is the wasteful nature of taxing commodities
even in this so-called free trade country; that
"it appears that to raise the revenue of sixty-
seven million under the present system, costs
the country £176,622,232, or upwards of 260
per cent. on the amount raised; and that to

raise the same amount under the new system
would cost the country only X 1,008,738 or 14
per cent. on the same amount raised, being
the cost of collection, showing an actual saving
to the country in money alone of £175,613,494
a year." Mr. FrELD might also correct himself
by referring to page 354-5 where he will find
that it is not as he states 4s. in the pound but
2s. in the pound, as property tax, and no poll
tax but a house tax that the author recom-
mends in the present edition.
As regards the difficulty of collecting the
Property Tax, I can only say that, as a pro-
perty holder, I have made no difficulty, and
don't believe anybody else would find it hard
to pay a Property Tax of 10 per cent., pro-
vided all the heavy burdens which make
living artificially dear were repealed, more
especially as the, repeal of indirect taxes
always tends to make "all classes prosperous,
and by that means recoup the propertied
men for the 10 per cent. tax.

I have written the above without communi-
cating with the author, and take the responsi-
bility on my own shoulders ;but if be has seen
Mr. FIELD'S letter, be is quite *able to answer
it if age and infirmity does not prevent him,
i.e., if he will condescend to do it.

articles.text:
CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ACTS.

1 'MINK MTS. WOLETTENIIOLME shows rather
too much readiness to convict me of ignorance
when she makes it appear that I said that a
woman was as safe from being mistaken by
the police for a prostitute as a man from being
hanged by mistake.
I did not require to be informed that a
woman charged with prostitution under these
acts was not committed for trial at the assizes,
nor yet had the benefit of counsel and jury.
My meaning was that absolute safety from
error is not attainable in this world for any

act of administration, and that any man is
liable even to be hanged by mistake, notwith-
Standing the extraordinary precautions taken
against such au error.
In the case Of the Acts it is obviously im-
possible that the same precautions can be
taken as in the
•case of people charged with
murder, or they would be unworkable, but if
Mrs. WOLSTENHOLME will take the trouble to
examine for herself into the precautions, arid
not be satisfied with reading the wild articles
in the Shield and aiitilar publications, she
will find that extraordinary care has been
taken to avoid mistakes on the part of the
police, and that it is all but impodsible, WI •
I believe quite impossible, for any woman to
be examined unless she be a bond fad prosti-
tute.

The opponents of the acts have exerted a
marvellous ingenuity in the way of their work-
ing. It is complained that there is no defini-
tion of what is a "common prostitute." If
any of your readers will go down to Portsmouth
and see the women who consort with the
sailors when a ship is being paid oil, they
would require no fine spun-definition of this
clue of persons, nor would they be so ready
to
.believe, with some ladies, that experienced
middle-aged. married police inspectors are
likely to err, and to mistake poor but respect-
able women for these foul-mouthed, gaudy,
brazen-faced harlots. Yet, poor creatures, bad
as their mode of life is, I would not leave
them wallowing in vice and disease, but bring
them within the pale of humanity by a little
wholesome coercion.

If, however, there be any sensible danger of
honest women being mistaken for prostitutes,
then by all means take further precautions.
To return to the oldillustration; if innocent men
were liable frequently to be hanged for murder,
there would be a strong case for improving
but none for repealing the law against murder.
In fine, I maintain that the laws have so far
worked admirably, and yet I should be de-
lighted if they could be improved, and made
superhumanly perfect.
But to argue with Mrs. W. and her party is
but beating the air, for she naively and in-
cautiously adds, "Perhaps he would be
astonished to learn that we should still object
to the acts, even could it be shown that they
involved no possible injury to innocent

women."

Indeed, I should not be astonished, for I
knew it beforehand.
Ever since these acts have been before the

Mrs. WOLSTENKOLUE says there are other

tr REPORT ON THE "NEW SOCIAL
MOVEMENT."
[PIIESENTED TO TEE POSITIVIST SOCIETY.]
HOWEVER small may be the practical results
to be expected from the new movement, it is
yet, from the Positive point of view, both
interesting and suggestive.
In the Past place, it is a social and not a
political movement, one, that is, which appeals
to social feelings, and not to political parties.
This is au important point for those who, like
ourselves, insist that the true nature of public
problems is essentially social. That a body of
aristocratic and working-class leaders should,
in organizing a new refer* pass out of the
111 sphere of political into that of social remedies
11 is eignificant. It is much more so when we
notice the interest which this has awakened in
Q 1 sections of the old parliamentary parties.
The 3310.filllent, too, differs from many others

in being so far coMprehensive as to embrace
many orders of remedies at once. To us, who
insist on the gradual and uniform raising of
the social system on all points, and reject all
special movements and all panaceas whatever,
this is hopeful and suggestive; but the pro-
giamme, though suggestive as a whole, omits
many points.of importance, and in our view
wholly *misconceives the true key of the solu-
tion, Le., the necessity of meeting moral evils
by moral, and not by political, remedies. In-
asmuch as the movement contemplates a solu-
tion of the seven problems by legislative inter-
ference, it is really most imperfect as a social
programme, and is unable to meet the criticism
of the ordinary economists.
To criticise the Seven Points in detail:—

(1). The notion of planting out the great cities
"into the clear" is chimerical, and would not
be desirable, if it were possible. The real
solution for the evils of overcrowded towns is
the gradual improvement of the buildings of
large cities, with Government assistance.
(2,) Self government in smaller circles is
scaecoly a gain in the eyes of those to whom:
mere self-government itself offers no hope.
T 1 residuum residuum of truth in this head is the need
of gradually concentrating political life into
small areas than those of existing European
nations.

(3.) Eight hours' labour for the day's work
would be in the spirit of Positivist maxims,
but it should not be by direct legislative

compulsion.
(4.) Public national schools accessible to all
also we adopt—only we add, provided they
are elementary and secular. _ . _

(5.) Public markets for sale of goods at
cost price—form certainly no part of the per-
manent function of Government, and are
possible only under special circumstances.
(6.) Public parks and libraries belong far
more to spiritual and voluntary agencies than
to legislation.
(7.) Railways, &c., to be purchased by the
State—may be desirable under conditions.

SUGGESTIONS FOR A PRACTICAL SOCIAL MOVE-
MENT PROM THE POSITIVIST POINT OP VIEW.
[This programme excludes all questions
that are strictly political, or deal with the distri-
bution of power, as well as all that are purely
moral, and appeal exclusively to religion or
feeling. 'The questions are therefore limited

to those in which public opinion may combine
with legislative aid in securing measures of
material social improvement, apart from party

or creed.]
POSTULATE.—The Positivist system pre-
supposes, as a coudition of all healthy social
life; the formation of an organized moral power
entirely independent of the State, and there-
fore in no sense a State Church, charged. with
the moral control and elevation of persons,

•
families, and institutions, with the task of all
higher education, and with the expression of
systematic public opinion. Without this,
Positivism declares all social movements

to be baseless. With this, and even
during its gradual formation, in some
degree as a step towards it, positivism does
favour the practical attempt to realize the parts
of a social programme, provided it be suffi-
ciently comprehensive, so as never to degener-
ate into specialism, and. sufficiently inspired
with moral aims, so as never to end in a more
political cry, e.g. :
(1.) Re-organize entirely the homes of the
working class both in town and country, the
aim being that the home of each labouring
family shall satisfy health, the conditions of
morality, decency, and, finally, of self-respect
and convenience for cultivated life.
N.B.—There is quite as much to be done in
the country, "out in the clear," as there is in

cities.
For this end it would be necessary largely
to rebuild such a city as London, so as to
eoonomise space by loftier buildings. This
vast work should be accomplished partly by
private enterprise or munificence, largely and
mainly by local municipal effort, partly as a
stimulus and example by the State, in all
cases assisted by State inspection, loans of
publio money, local Acts, tte., &e. In the
end, it is essential that the workman, in town
or country, should own, his house in full
property. The State and publie bodies may
assist this ends but it is mainly a duty do

volving upon true capitalists, and already
recognised by sOme of them. The wcrkman
can never be a free man or a full citizen until
his home is his own—a castle really sacred
from private or publio oppression.
(2.) All this requires to be aided by an
unceasing application of public power to the
sanitary condition in all its phases. Health
ought to be at once a State department, in-
cluding therein, first, the negative require-
ments of removal of nuisances, of stopping
infection and contagion, the rigorous suppres-
sion of all adulteration in articles of food,
&e.; secondly, the positive task of securing
adequate fresh air, numerous and accessible
grounds for recreation, and a supply Of fault-
less water. Most of this can be left to local
municipal effort, and even private munificence.
But it is the undoubted function of the central
Power to see that these ends are attained, and
to provide all the assistance it can towards
, their attainment.

(3.) Pending the gradual formation of
smaller local centres, much may be done at
once by the State, and more by municipal and
private effort, to give provincial centres some
of those intellectual and artistic advantages,
and some of that crgatic life which is already
bestowed on the metropolis. It was very re-
pressive of free national life, that the educa-
tional and tosthetio resources of the Nation
should be concentrated on London. Much has
to be done to stimulate public life, and to re-
vive education and independence in our ancient
cities, which are too :often sacrificed to the
seat of Government.

(4.) The shortening of the hours of labour
to eight hours per diem may at once be made
a social movement. Positivism has its own
measure for this want, but one for which the
industrial system is as yet unprepared. But
the conviction that the present working hours
are excessive, measured by the requirements
of health, education, and citizenship, is one
which it is of vital importance to spread. This
applies, not merely to factory labour, but to
agricultural and even domestic labour. But
it must be arrived at by free agreement of
both parties; but the State might preperly
aid by the adoption of the Eight Hours' Act
of the 'United States, by reducing the hours to
eight in the Government employment of all
kinds—dockyards, post-office, kto., etc.—and
might require it in all 'eases where overwork
becomes injurious or dangerous to others, e. 11.,
on railways and in mines.

(5.) But shorter hours will not avail without
simultaneous efforts to free women and children
from the excessive and more injurious forms
of public labour. Opinion should be at once
organised to put an end to the systematic work
of women in factories, as being for all
married woman incompatible with their com-
monest duty, and for unmarried women
injurious to moral and physical life, and in
all cases antagonistic to the true spirit of
family life. The work of children should be
gradually reduced (by statute) until, by the
effect of opinion and law, tlio emiiloyment of
all young persons is reduced to the bona fide
learning of a trade, and does not interfere
with education or health.

(6.) Public holidays. In addition to Sun-
day and the Saturday half-holiday, which
might at once be made universal, much has
to be done. Public holidays should be at
least one a month. This may be effected by
the combined influence of opinion and law, the
former preceding the latter.
(7.) Clubs. It is essential for the full
citizenship of the workmen that they should
have ht and attractive clubs for social and
political discussion. This is a legitimate
subject for municipal though not for State in-
tervention, though it must mainly depend on
private munificence and the energy of work-
men themselves.
• (8.) Instruction should be national, primary
gratuitous, and secular, with unlimited free-
dom of teaching and discoursing to all persons
or bodies. And for this purpose it is very
desirable that the Municipalities should afford
suitable localities,
(9,) An earnest handling of the licensing
system. Under the present system, which
practically puts public houses into -the Imo
controlled. power of a powerful order palm..
ntarlly intereatid in than, every form Of oat=

rUption exists. Official supervision of public-
houses is desirable, provided it ho limited to
the maintenance of order, and the suppression
of adulteration, but it must be free from any
form of political interference. Whilst we do
not favour the present undue mult ipliezit ion of
public-houses, beer-shops or gin-palaces our
end would rather be to improve than to sup-
press. We should prefer a return to the
older and more sociable form of public-house
to the present odious bar-aYstem—that is, a
spasm Which offered the means of rest; food,
and intercourse; in place of orte of which the
sole object is drink.
(10.) Social moiement, assisted by State
guarantees, for the transference of aitistio,
scientific, or literary treasures from private to
to public enjoyment,' e. g., the State might
assist and opinion might urge possessors of
pictures, or libraries, &el., to dedicate, them:
under stated conditions, to the public, i.e.,
revival of the noble system of antiquity, the
" Leiturgies," or public 'gifts of rich and
eminent citizens, who dedicated their fortunes
to the public enjoyment and instruction.
Thus the higher form of park, museum,
• library, So., would be supplied by private
Munificence, without any direct State 'inter-
ference beyond that of encouragement end
guarantee.

(11.) Entire re-organisation of public service
—docks, factories; post-office, and lel ministra-
tive departments—on the principle' of exel tiding
competition in wages ; and, instead of making
public employes public slaves, providing that
the service of the State should be a typo of
good employment. Under the existing system
many of the inferior servants of the State, in
docks, post-off Ace, &c., aro ill-used, over-
worked, and underpaid. The permanence and
certainty of public service form a reasonable
attraction. This advantage it is for the
interest of the State to use, by obtaining
superior servants, and not by saving in reduc-
tion of 'wages.
(12.) Transference of all roads, railways,
harbours, piers, docks, bridges, lighthouses,
&c., &0., and all other works open to. common
use of all travelling by sea or land, to the
State, to be worked on the system above; and
estieciatlY excluding all competition in wage,
an all parey economic objects at the ex ;
tieills(4lOf Vublio convenience, and the welfare
or tlli' iii lio servant.
le
(11.) The evils of the system of poor relief
appear to us very complex, and in fact to
underlie the whole industrial system. We
see no method of effectually redressing the
evils of that system, without abrogating the
right to State relief. But the mode in which
this alone 'could be accomplished, and the
methods of dealing with exceptional destitu-
tion require a special report whieli will
shortly be presented.

QUESTIONS BY A POSITIVIST.

TWELFTH QUESTION.—Is WA OWEN find his
system forgotten? Is it at all likely that the
dead can be raised, or flesh and life given to
dry bones?

.A.riswEn.—lt is shown most plainly by this
and the preceding questions that our Positivist
friends are not aware of the nature and results
of the educational experiments of the great
English social reformer—that they are not
acquainted with the knowledge upon which
the new system is based, and that they have
most vague and erroneous ideas of the details
of the system. But in this they are only in
the same position as the world in general.
' And it is well that they have not endeavoure4
to obtain the information which they need
from the writings of Mr. OWEN. For if they
had done so they would have failed, as others
have failed, to obtain it. And they,eannot be
blamed for rejecting without examination a
system which has been justly condemned by
public opinion as unsound. But now that the
just grounds of this condemnation have been
removed, they will be neglecting an urgent
and imperative duty, to themselves and to the
public, if they remain uninformed upon this
'subjeot, and if in consequence they continue
to misapply their exertions as men who desire
to knew and to enable others to knew the
means by which alone the moral and plipical
evils of the present state of society may be
remedied. 'No one who desires the vrell4.being

and happiness of his fellow men will know-
ingly waste his energies to endeavouring to
disseminate ideas which can never lead to the
right course for the realisation of the three
great wants of sooiety, which I have repeatedly
named—character, wealth, and beneficial in-
stitutions and arrangenfents, for all.

OWEN is not, and never will be, forgotten.
And his system is not a dead thing, which can
not be resuscitated. itis aliving and vigorous
germ . of a magnificent new tree, which will
bear in profusion the fruit of happiness for
mankind. A. powerful obstruction has hitherto
prevented its development. But this impedi-
ment is now removed, and nothing now can
prevent its growth and propagation, until
the inhabited earth is beautified and made
delightful by its presence. My Positivist
friend concludes with the

THIRTEEN= QUESTION.---a If it can" (that
is, if "the dead can be raised," &c., see
Twelfth Question), "must it not be by a
vigorous agitation lectures, discussions,
tracts, and a living and active association of
mn eminent for intellectual power, position,
- and moral character ? "

ANS'WEIL.--It is quite true, and is well
known, that the Means stated in this question
are the proper means for the effectual dis-
semination of correct views of Social Reform.
But we have had first to obtain the correct
views, and to arrange them intelligibly. The
next step is to make them public, to some
extent, by means of the press, and by replying,
by the same means, to the questions of the
uninformed. (Not by " discussions " with
them, so far as our subject is ascertained. We
need not " discuss " what is known, with
those who do not know it; and with those who
know it there will be no wish for. discussion.
The chemist does not discuss the ascertained
facts of chemistry with those who do not
know them.) And sufficient preparation must
be made by these means before we ban usefully
form a "living and active association." "In-
tellectual power, and position, and moral
character," without the knowledge which
atone can give true enlightenment and enable
men to acquire enlightened, goodness, can
never produce an effective association for the
remedy of our social evils. But it will also
be necessary to have a practical example of
the new system for the World to see, before
the great majority Of the old world
"thinkers" will be able to free themselves
from the erroneous and injurious habits of
thought and feeling which , they, have been
caused to acquire by the influences of the old
system. This example will be equally effica-
cious, whether it is realised under the direc-
tion of a few wealthy subseribersnf capital for
the purpose, or 'even of one wealthy individual,
or by means Of a numerous body of contri-
butors of small sums. The" fact that the
system may be introduced extensively while
. those who do not wish to enter into it remain
undisturbed in their present positions, and
that it can only be realized .in the spirit of
good will to all, upon which it will be based,
is a circumstance most favourable to its pro-
ess. And as we have new 'obtained the re-
quired knowledge, there cannot be any
reasonable doubt that all the rest will follow
in due time..

In another paper I will give a short account
of the discovery and verification of the know-
ledge upon which, with the enlightened good-
ness which it will produce, the co-operative
ocial system will be 'based. This Will ho
useful to Overcome the difficulty which is ex-
perienced by some enquirers (as we. lately Saw
in Mr: nsitToN's remarks), in discerning the
good effects which will result. in man's
character, &0., from the understanding of the
fundamental truth which is the basis of the
knowledge of the causes of evil, and of good to
man, and from the acquirement of this know-
ledge; and the evil effectsWhioh have resulted
from the denial of this truth, in the erroneous
part of the common idea of free-will, and from
ignorant° of these causes; and to make evident
the fatal deficiency of all projects of social re-
form in which the vital importance of this
knowledge (including, of course, the. under-
standing of the truth upon which it is based),
is not distinctly recognised.

THE WOMAN'S DISABILITIES BILL.
Tura Bill having been rejected a fourth
time, may I venture very briefly to point out
the one vital and. fundamental objection to its
re-appearance in its present form. It inflicts
a gross injustice upon married women, who
have as good a right to the suffrage as spin-
sters, the rates, &c., notwithstanding. For
let us consider the essential meaning of
property qualifications as they are understood
by the great majority of the Liberal party.
They have by us been hitherto regarded in the
light of tests, mental fitness, guarantees of
personal capacity for the discharge of electoral
duties. It may be conceded that the Reform
Acts of 1832 and 1867 effected their avowed
object, viz., the enfranchisement of the pre-
sumably most enlightened men in the middle
and working ranks respectively upon whom
the vote was conferred, not because they paid
local rates, not so much because they con-
tributed to the Imperial Revenue, but upon
large and comprehensive views of public justice
and public expediency. Very well, then. If
the qualification, which as far as male electors
are concerned, is fairly satisfactory, be utterly
inadequate, when you come to deal with the
question of admitting within the political pale
a class, the flower of which devotes itself
primarily to indoor , rather than outdoor
labour, to domestic rather than to professional
functions, to money saving rather than to
money earning, does it not appear to be wise
that we should endeavour so to amend the
qualification as to meet the difficulties of the
case? Will any one pretend that rate-paying
single ladies are more deserving of this trust
than the wives of members of the House of
Commons, than Mrs. FAWCETT, for example, or
Mrs. GLADSTONE ? No, Sir, if any women
merit the franchise more than others, it is
just the very persons whom this precious
spinster's Bill proposes to exelude. Upon the
average, it can hardly be denied that the
married woman who comes into contact with
her husband's pursuits and habits of thought,
who generally sees more of the world, and who,
to quote the words of the Times newspaper,
has a "more full experience of life," is a
more intelligent member of society, and there-
fore more likely to give a reflecting vote than
persons who at present are wont to pass their
days in a somewhat too unobtrusive and
secluded fashion. It is foolishly asserted in
some quarters thatwheniNfr. RUSSELL GURNEY'S
Bill is placed ou the statute book, these matters
would le set straight for married women, but
if those who make such statements would only
take the trouble to look a little deeper, they
might discover the whimsical fallacies of the
argument. Suppose, in the first place, that
house property were left to one's wife, and it
were not unjustly merged, to use a polite
legal phrase, in 'the estate of the husband,
in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred,
the parties would not keep up two estab-
lishments, but the wife would sell the
house, and invest the proceeds of the sale in
railway stook or other securities of that de-
scription. She is therefore disfranchised for
acting in accordance with the practical rules
of wedded life. Or, suppose it to be more con-
venient that the husbandli: should close his
establishment, and migrate to the wife's pre-
mises, then, inasmuch as her name is on the
rate-book, he loses hi vote, and the maxim
"Once a voter always a voter" is laughed to
scorn. Doubtless the two Bills taken together
would emancipate a few married women free-
holders in counties, but how atrociously unfair
that female residents in towns should be
debarred from a trust, which they are equally
competent to exercise for the good of the corn.
plunity. To my mind, there is something
extremely repulsive in the undue importance
attached, or rather professedly attributed, on
Woman's Rights platforms to the burdens of
taxation, forsooth, under which spinsters are
supposed to groan, as though married women,
who have had money settled upon them through
the intervention of trustees, married women
who pay bills, and keep the house accounts, had
not a precisely similar stake in the material
prosperity of the Country. It is alleged, with
what degree of truth I leave your readers to
judge, that spinsters are liable to obligations
from which our wives are exempt; but is it
not obvious that those who undergo the pains

and perils of childbirth, who train up healthy
and virtuous children in the service of God
and their country, fulfil duties of citizenship
infinitely more solemn than the comparatively
speaking paltry liabilities of women whose
position in the State is, I am forced to say it,
much less important, less onerous, less re-
sponsible? Again, who are the women who,
under the existing barbarous state of the law,
are exposed to the danger of being stripped of
their property, of being robbed of their children,
of being deprived by a drunken ruffian of that
pecuniary sustenance which, in consideration
of a hard day's work in the house and other
reeiprocal offices of love and duty, they are
morally, though not legally entitled? Why it
is the married women who labour under these
acknowledged grievance:, and yet it is pro-
posed to limit the suffrage to persons who stand
less in need of it as a protection. Then it is
reasonably contended that women's votes are
required in order to humanize polities, that is,
to infuse into our legislation those qualities of
tenderness, gentleness, and forbearance in
which we men are perhaps rather deficient.
But are married women less gentle, andless eel
passionate for the sufferings of the poor C.,
their unmarried sisters? It is urged, morec•- dr,
that indirect influence is baneful. Quite true, as
a matter of fact, the husband from want of
intellectual and spiritual sympathy at home
is frequently tempted to yield to the perni-
bious influences of the employer, the union,
the landlord, the customer, the tradesman, &0.,
while if his wife were taught to interest her-
self in public affairs, he would often, though
exposed to exactly the same temptation, be
encouraged to stand firm against the insidious
pressure. But if this argument applies to single
ladies, how much more is it applicable to the
married, who have numberless opportunities
of wielding that power which we are told
ought as far as is practicable, to be co exten-
sive with responsibility.
Now it may be said, there may be some
truth in all this, but there are grave difficulties
in the way of enfranchising married women,
which are absent in our little modest one clause
bill. To this I reply, lotus boldly, consistently,
and honourably grapple with those difficulties.
I for one, firmly believe that in six or eight
years' time the men of this country, no matter
what the rank to which they belong, will be
prepared to make a generous conoession of
political liberty to women. We shall soon
appreciate to its full extent the glorious truth,
that charity begins at home, and we husbands
shall in the course of a little time be reluctant
to extend popular rights out of doors
while acquiescing in the faintest sem-
blance, whether in law or practice, of a
despotism in our own families. I object to
the Disabilities Bill, not because it is a so-called
moderate reform, for I strenuously deny that
thatmeasure is animprovement which virtually
imposes a fresh civil disability upon married
women who have done nothing to deserve
such a cruel punishment, and which is, in the
opinion of the Daily Telejraph in which I
heartily coincide, a premium upon Coe, inso-
far as a kept mistress who pays her rates
would be entrusted with a privilege which is
denied to the virtuous and chaste matron.
Away, then, with this wretched Bill, which
seeks to degrade the most hallowed. and
tender of human relationships, which seeks to
render marriage, the holy covenant of matri-
mony, a badge of political disgrace, a signifi-
cant emblem of civic dishonour! Let us
postpone the suffrage agitation until the time
is ripe for an honest measure, enfranchising a
fair proportion of married and single women.
Opinions may of course differ as to the details
of such a scheme. For my own part, I could
conscientiously support a Bill which gave
the vote to women in what are called the
upper and. middle ranks alone to begin with.
I look upon female suffrage as a democratic
vote, politically speaking, no matter what the
station of society in which the woman
may chance to move; and, therefore, I
think we could with perfect consistency
and with much indisputable benefit to the
working classes, enfranchise some time or
other the as it were lower scale, if I may use
snoh an expression, female members of the
professional grades, at the same time that we
extend. the suffrage to the male agricultural

labourer. For the present, the National
Suffrage Society might be content with
moderate educational and other reforms, all
steps in the right direction, and not force
upon public attention an utterly indefensible
and preposterous proposal, which very few of
its defenders are able to uphold without a
quasi-judicious adjustment of that muzzle
which is anything but conducive to a sincere
and honourable advocacy, and which in the
clearly expressed estimation of Parliament,
the press, and the country, tends to create the
most odious, invidious, and insulting distinc-
tions between married and unmarried women.
Luria TuoErrol{ Howls.
Reform Club.

articles.text:
THE LONDON. SCHOOL BOARD.

On Wednesday, the usual weekly meeting
of this Board was held at the Guildhall, Mr.
Charles Reed, M.P., presiding. Mr. Watson
presented a report from the Statistical
Committee, which proposed to transfer the
Field-lane Ragged Schools to the Board, and
moved that the boys' and girls' school on the
second floor be taken from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. on
the six days of the week for one year, the Board
to pay £l5O per annum as a proportionate share
of the total outgoings. This gave rise to some
discussion, the chairman giving it as his
opinion that the subject should go back to the
committee, and the solicitor to the Board
stating that the Education Department would
wuold not allow any payment 'which
be in the nature of a profit rent. On a
livision the recommendation in the report was
carried by 20 to 4. On the motion of the
chairman a report of the Works and General
Purposes Committee, relating to the acquisi-
tion of sites for new schools, was adopted. A
recommendation of the School Management
Committee that the reading books used in all
board schools should be provided by the Board,
was carried; but other reeommendations of the
same committee relating to the cost of station
-
cry and apparatus, were referred back for
further consideration. After the transaction
of some other business the Board adjourned.

A. case was heard before Vice-Chancellor
Wickens on Tuesday, in which a shareholder in.
the Smyrna and Aidin line of the Ottoman Rail-
way sought to compel the directors to refund
such ot the company's money as had been
expended in prosecuting a Mr. ElEssen for
libel. The alleged libel was embodied in
some representations to Lord Stanley, when
Foreign Secretary, in 1868, urging him to
warn the Turkish Government not to pay a
promised guarantee to the directors, inasmuch
as it would be misapplied, and the majority of
the shareholders had sanctioned the expendi-
ture of the company's funds, which was now
complained of. The Vice-Chancellor, while
declining to make any order with reference to
costs incurred before the institution of this
suit, granted a perpetual injunction against
any future payments of a like character.

articles.title: TUB CLOTH PRESSERS AND DRESSES.
articles.text:
TUB CLOTH PRESSERS AND DRESSES.

The dispute between the cloth pressers and
their employers as to the length of pieces to be
pressed seems to be approaching its close. Their
application for an increase of payment according
to the length of the piece has been favourably
entertained by 42 fiims; only one firm has positively
refused to entertain their application, and the rest
of their employers have agreed to be ruled by the
decision of the other employers. We understand
that the cloth dressers are taking action respecting
the adjustment of the lengths of pieces they are
required to dress. At a meeting of the operatives
in the Old Assembly Rooms, it was resolved that
the masters should be requested to appoint a
deputation from their body to meet a deputation
from the operatives. The masters have agreed to
meet the deputation.

articles.text:
TUE TRADES COUNCIL.

The usual monthly meeting of the Leeds and
District Trades Council was held on Wednesday
last, at Parker's Temperance llotel. Representa-

G. IL Carpenters and Joiners; Amalgamated

makers, Clothdressers, Engineers, Ironfounders,
Shoemakers (Rivetters and Finishers), Tailors,

It was resolved that a committee of five be
appointed for the purpose of revising the same,
and prepare their report by tho next monthly

After discussing" the cases tried under the

groat pleasure the introduction by the Government

NORTH AMPTON.
THE SHOEMAKERS' STRIKE,

The strike of the shoemakers of Northampton
(the Amalgamated Society of Shoemakers) com-
menced an extensive organization on January 1,
1872, the Executive Council engaged Mr. G.
Odger to deliver a course of lectures in North-
ampton and the county on capital labour and
trades unions, with special reference to the shoo
trade. The numbers of the society previous to the
organization were few compared to the numbers
working at the trade. We have enrolled great
numbers in the town and county. On March 29
we issued memorials and classified lists of the ad-
vance we requested, giving the employers nearly a
month's notice. The men met to receive and con-
sider the answers. The advance offered was—all
work under eighteenpenco one penny, from
eighteenpenco to half-a-crown twopence, and all
above threepence per pair. After a lengthy dis-
cussion, the men finally agreed to abide by the
statement, giving the employers till the 25th of
April. Those shops not complying be declared
on strike, and the men be drawn off forthwith, the
employers be made acquainted of the same. The
men were willing to arbitrate the question, but the
employers would not treat with them. A letter
was sent to the employers' association, stating that
a deputation would attend their meeting if re-
quested, so that if any difficulties should arise they
might be satisfactorily adjusted. To this we
received no answer. A largo number of the men
have left the town; they still continuo leaving
daily. Since the commencement of the strike
thirty-two shops have given in, and acknowlege
the Society.—Yours most truly, signed on behalf
of the United Committee,

DARLINGTON.
TUE IRON TRADE.

The North of England Iron Trade Arbitration
Board, which sat for two days at Darlington, with
Mr. Rupert Kettle as arbitrator, concluded its
sittings on Friday, when Mr. Kettle decided that
the men should be relieved from fettling and all
other work on Sundays, and also that there should
be a provisional arrangement to the end of the
year, when the masters can re-open the question if
there be loss of heats and less iron produced ; that
the puddlers shall commence work at five, not
changing furnaces after three o'clock morning and
evening.

DERBY.
STRIKE OF SILK SPINNERS.

The principal silk mills at Derby were closed on
Saturday morning owing to a strike of the spin-
ners, Last Saturday the spinners sent in notices
to their employers that unless their application for
an advance of 2s. per week was granted they
would cease work on Thursday night. On Tues-
day notices were posted at the factories stating
that, in consequence of the step which had been
taken by the spinners, the mills would not be opened
to any hard silk hands on Saturday morning.

articles.title: STATEMENT OF THE OPERATIVES.
articles.text:
STATEMENT OF THE OPERATIVES.

The same old style.; no improvement; time and
experience have taught them nothing; made them
no wiser. The masters of the manufactories here
have begun to use a contentions iron-hand way of
dealing. They have threatened all those men
whose families are employed at the same place,
that if they do not immediately return to work
and disband themselves from the union, neither
they nor any of their families shall be permitted to ,
enter the place again; and they are allowed to
assume, "or in any other place in the. town," as
the masters are united together. Why, Sir, every
person must know, by the language they use, that
the masters are already, or nearly, beaten. Every
reader or person that has had the slightest experi-
ence in strikes, can see the desperation of the
threat—which tells its own tale—is one which
they never will, and, perhaps, never had any
intention of carrying into effect. But the men at
. present are as firm as they were when they first
passed the resolution to have the advance ; and I
believe their families are as resigned, and ready to
accept what time may bring forth.
On Monday evening there was a crowded and
most enthusiastic meeting of both sexes, and the
spinners were all determined to keep out until
the masters granted the required advance.
Money is coming in from all quarters in large
sums, and there is every likelihood that the men
will be supported in a better manner than they
over expected.

It is surprising, Sir, with what authority and
contemptuousness of right your provincial con-
temporaries take the matter up, pointing out what
they used to have in days so long gorse by, and
altogether ignoring the slightest thought of what
they should have, according to the amount of the
profitable work they do.
Thera agam, Sir, is the same old argument that
has ever been used by upholders of a wrong
cause. If these ill-paid workmen wore once
receiving wages thAt an honest and honourable
master might well blush to offer them—though I
have not heard that one ever did—and if they
have slightly improved their former state, but are
still short of their rights, is it any sound or reason-
able argument, Sir, that they should still remain
satisfied with less than rightful remuneration for
their labour, and less than theii, fellow-workmen
are receiving? No, Sir, it is a wrong idea
altogether. It may do for these gold mania
scribblers to talk amongst themselves, or with
those old-fogie masters that lived in the last
century, but it will not stand as a fair and just
argument at the present day.
Taking these things into consideration, and the
fact that they arc now doing double the quantity
of work they were when wages were so low—and
I can vouch for the accuracy of this statement—
think, Sir, that the men are but struggling for
what is their own by the rights Of justice and
labour.

If one s.couses the men of being somewhat
hatitYs we ;Awt. alsotalco. into oeuisider4tvion that

it is the masters that have driven them to it, and
left them no alternative but to do so. Had they
promised to consider the matter, the men might
have accepted a compromise, then the worst of
this serious affair would have been warded off,
and this feudal struggle would not now be
rankling in the breasts or both master and man.

HANLEY.
THE IHONWOHRERS.

A meeting of the ironworkers of North Stafford-
shire washeld on Monday in the Temperance Hall,
Hanley. The meeting was attended by several
delegates from other parts of the country.

Mr. Richard Jones, of Stockton, moved a
resolution in favour of the adoption of a uniform
basis of wages all over the country, which was
seconded by Mr. A. Walker, of Tipton, and sup-
ported by Mr. James Capper, of Bloxwich.
The next resolution (moved by a local, iron-
worker), proposed that a conference should be held
in Sheffield on Whit Monday and Tuesday, ith
view to strengthening the union of ironworkers.
This was seconded by Mr. Cope, of Spennymoor.
Mr. john Kane, of Darlington, moved a resolu-
tion expressing strong disapproval of the conduct
of the Government and the House of Commons in
referring the Wages Bill to a secret select com-
mittee, sitting with closed doors, and refusing to
receive evidence or take counsel from the working
classes, whose practical knowledge of the abuses
of the Truck Act enabled them to give useful
evidence upon the subject. In the course of his
address Mr. Kane advocated weekly payments of
wages, no stoppages, and the basing of wages
upon the average of all classes of work. Mr. A.
A. Walton, of Brecon, supported the proposal,
urging upon the ironworkers the advantages of
union, bolding out as an ultimate object to be aimed
at co-operative proprietorship. All the resolu-
tions were passed unanimously, and a vote of
thanks was accorded to the delegates who were
in attendance.

abolition of the system of deductions from their
