articles.title: STRIKE Of CARrENTEfIe AND JOINERS.
articles.text:
STRIKE Of CARrENTEfIe AND JOINERS.

Three hundred of the carpenters and joiners of
Nottingham came out on strike on Monday last.
The cause of the dispute is as follows :—ln
December last notice was given by the operatives
for a re-adjustment of the working time, and an
advance of one halfpenny per hour. The time for
the past two years has been 55 hours for 40 weeks,
and 47 hours for 12 weeks, or a weekly average
for the year of 63 hours. It was proposed by the
workmen that the time should be uniform
throughout the year, 62i hours. No attempt
having been made by the employers before the
beginning of April to effect a settlement. A
meeting was arranged to be held on April 17th,

when it was decided to give the proposed
advance on condition of the workmen accepting
the time made by masons and bricklayers, less
one hour than at present worked for the longer
period, 55 hours, viz., 64 hours for 35 weeks, 50
hours for 6 weeks, and 42 hours for n weeks in
a year. This proposition, when brought before
the operatives, was unanimously rejected, and a
notification to this effect directed to be sent to
the employers through their secretary, and also an
intimation that six of the workmen were appointed
to meet six of the employers. At the meeting the
men brought forward this proposition, along with
an alternative (in case of non-acceptance) to work
the present time at the same rate as bricklayers,
or 7fd. per hour. This last was not entertained,
and no satisfactory result accruing, each side were
left in the same position as before the meeting
was held. A general feeling of dissent from the
proposed time having been evinced, and many
employers stating their intention to give the
advance on condition that the time was not altered,
and the operatives still feeling desirous to effect an
amicable arrangement instead of a strike, an
aggregate meeting of the three societies was
held. at the Mechanics' Hall on Friday even-
evening, May 3rd, when 500 members were pre-
sent. The following resolution being unanimously
passed That in view of a settlement of the
present dispute, this meeting agrees that in shops
wore the employers are willing to give the advance
of one halfpenny per hour, the time to-remain as
at present; we accept the same and allow the men
in such shops to remain at work." It was under-
stood that this resolution, amounting as it did to a
withdrawal of the uniform weekly time, would be
generally accepted, but the result proved other-
wise, as on Saturday many employers expressed
their determination to adhere to the original pro-
position of the shorter time in winter, both for
shops and buildings, and also discharging some of
the men, others not going so far as this who were
willing for the advance and the time as at present.
But at a general meeting of the employers it had
been agreed that all should be guided by a resolu-
tion not to swerve from their own offer. They con-
sequently were not individually willing to recede
therefrom until a general meeting had decided upon
the course of action. On Monday morning, when
the roll of operatives out on strike, had been called
over, it was found that .out of a total of 600 in the
town and district, 300 were on strike and the same
number at work on the men's terms. Two meet-
ings of the employers have been held this week,
but, as showing that they themselves alone, and not
the men, are desirous to continue the strike,
they are trying to persuade or mildly coerce
those employers whose men are at work to dis-
charge or lock-out their men until we have agreed
to such a revision of the working rules as will
amount to a virtual acceptance of their terms.
This they, with a unanimity to be commended for,
object to, as to force one branch of the building
trade to work shorter hours; when full time could
be made in shops to suit the convenience of
employers and the other branches would be a gross
'nj natio°.

articles.title: STAFFORDSHIRE POTTERIES.
articles.text:
STAFFORDSHIRE POTTERIES.

TILE YLAP PRESSEiIB.
The following has been sent to the Parlia-
mentary and Select Committee of the House of
Commons on the Truck Bill:
" GENTLEMEN,—It is the wish of the Flat
Pressers' Society that a clause should be inserted
in the Truck Bill to do away with the system of
good from oven,' which we have to suffer front
in our trade. The abominations of the Truck
system cannot be worse than ours, In many
instances after a man's work has gone through
the fire, and he is in full expectation of seeing it
good, so as to be paid for it, he does not see more
than half or two-thirds, good and bad together.
It has to be looked over oven then by the person
in the biscuit waro-roorn, and counted afterwards
to the man in the following order, viz., 121 doz.
of plates good, 35 doz. general seconds, 14 doz. ,
crooked, 4i doz. cracked or nipped, 3 doz. bad;
thus out of 1771 doz. tho man would get paid
about 130 doz., the others being a dead loss to
him. Many such cases can be cited at the same
manufactory. Another case of a man at another
manufactory had (Feb. 17, 1872) 107 doz. of
plates to be paid for, but when sent for
to count his ware, he received 18 doz. out of
the 107 doz., the other 89 doz. no one
knew anything about them. On the 24th Fob.,
1872, this same man had 298 doz. passing through
the fire, and when they got in the ware-room 23
doz. were missing altogether, and because the man
spoke aboutit his employer condemned the rest, and
and would not pay him for them because they
were bad, consequently the man was a fortnight
without wages. Another case where two dish-
makers had '2OO doz. of dishes put on one side as
being bad, but in a short time some of these dishes

were wanted to make up a package (not as bad
but as good ware), one man was made a present
of ten shillings, and the other twenty shillings,
not to take any further notice; in this way the
men wore diddled out of about four pounds. We
have had several cases in the County Court, which
have been decided in the men's favour, but all the
men have not got the courage to commence actions
in law, if they had the means. We might go on
enumerating hundreds of cases similar to the
above, but we think they will suffice for the
present. In closing this account of this abomin-
able system allow us to say that some manufac-
turers are worse than others. At some
manufactories, men, women, and children
go into the ware-room, take the first they
want, such as plates, dishes, and saucers by doz.,
wash bowls, nay any other article they may stand
in need of, the same not having been counted to
the workman; and when he complains that he is
some work short, he is told that it is not come
there, that it has not been made, that it is ix the
ball clay heap, that it is at Runcorn, nay, it has
flown out at the "top of the oven." Thus the
man having received such taunts as these is com-
pelled to bear the loss, unless he is determined to
make enquries elsewhere. Under the system of
"good from oven," men are subject to many bits
of petty tyranny that other trades do not ex-
perience, and if a clause like the following could
be inserted at the end of section 6, it would be a
great boon to all potters, viz. :—That all ware be
paid "good from hand," that the same be counteJ
by the master, manager, or foreman, when it is
finished and ready for the kiln, and paid for on the
Saturday in each week, without any abatement or
stoppage whatever, arid to be paid in the current
coin of the realm. .

"By order of the Flat Pressers' Executive Com-
mittee."

• WOLVERHAMPTON.
ARBITRATION IN THE BUILDING TRADES.

A meeting of the building trades was held last
week in the Grand Jury Room, at the Town Hall,
under the presidency of Mr. Rupert Kettle, County
Court Judge of Worcestershire. The carpenters
and joiners and bricklayers had given notice for an
advance from (lid. to 7d. per hour, and the work-
ing hours to be reduced from 561 to 54 hours per
week; and the plasterers had, demanded a rise from
6id. to 7id. per hour, and a raduction in the work.
lug hours from 56i to 50i hours. The masters
were represented by Messrs. George Highatn,
Henry Lovett, John Cockerill, Frederick Higham,
George Heveninghatn, and Reubin Burkitt ; the
carpenters and joiners' representatives being
Messrs. John Jeavons, Thomas Miles, George
Barratt, William Wellings, Frank Jarrett, and
Joseph Hall.
It was moved, seconded, and carried unani-
mously that the rate of wages be advanced one-
halfpenny per hour, increasing them to sevenpence,
and the working hours reduced to 64 per week.
After a short discussion, it was agreed that the
alteration should take effect on the Ist of May,
and continue in force for three years—that is,
until May, 1876.

Mr. Kettle suggested that occasional meetings of
both masters and men should be held, as a means
of bringing them into contact with each other, and
improving the good feeling already existing.
The operative bricklayers were next introduced.
The men were represented by Messrs. Henry
Cheese, James Shutt, John Addenbrook, William
Hallett, Joseph Taylor, and John Beddow. The
rise asked for, being the same as.the carpenters,
was granted by the masters without diecussion,
and the hours reduced—both parties binding them-
selves for three years, as in the previous ease.
The plasterers then came forward; the men con-
sisting of Messrs. William Kennedy, Thomas
MacDonald, Henry Pitt, Richard Price, Donald
MacDonald, and Edward Drane. After a brief
conversation, in which it was urged how desirable
it would be, after paying them the same wages as

„
the carpenters and bricklayers, to advance them
oue farthing over the others and to disturb as
nine hours system, it was determined unanimously
that the rate of wages be advanced to 7d. per hour,
and tho time reduced to 54 hours, which should
constitute a week's work, the arrangement to con-
tinue in force until May, 1875.
Votes of thanks in each case were passed to the
learned umpire for his kindness and courtesy.

NA NTWICII.
TERMINATION OV THE LOC:E-OUT IN THE SHOE
TRADE.

The lock-out here in the shoe trade has been
brought to an amicable close ,the employers recognis-
ing our Society, and agreeing to an uniform state-
ment of wages, an advantage unprecedented in our
town, to which must be added that the above
statement includes a rise in the average of at least
10 per cent, On behalf of our aociety accept

our sincere thanks for the apace afforded to our
appeal in your valuable paper. It is our duty and
wish to increase its circulation. We have resolved
to add 24 copies weekly to the circulation here,
and shall do our utmost to increase that number
speedily, which you will know through our
newsagent.

JoRN Snacox.

MANCHESTIM.
THE THREATENED STRIKE OF BAKERS.
A meeting of the Committee of the Amalga-
mated Union of Bakers was held at the White
Hart, Ancoats-lane, on Tuesday evening, when it
was resolved to adhere to the resolution passed at
the public meeting held in the Memorial Hall the
previous week—namely, if the masters did not
concede the demands of the men, to give notice on
the 4th and come out on strike on the 11th inst.
It was also decided that the employes of those
masters who had granted the advance of wages
and a reduction in the hours of labour should can-
tinue at their employment and not come out with
the others.

articles.title: HUDDERSFIELD.
articles.text:
HUDDERSFIELD.

THE CARPENTERS AND JOINERS.

The excitement which has been prevalent
amongst the operative carpenters and joiners,
since the issue of their notice in October last,
asking bra reduction of their hours from 52. i to
50 hours per we?k, and an advance of 4s. per
week wages, was brought to a close without any'
outbreak of feeling on either side. This very'
satisfactory ending to what at one time threatened
to be a bitter struggle is no doubt greatly
indebted to the influence of the Joiners' and Car-
penters' Board of Arbitration and Conciliation for
Huddersfield and district, which already during
the short time it has been established, has proved
itself of incalculable value in arbitrating upon
any disputes which have arisen between masters
and men.

The delegates of the operatives had a difficult
task before them, the masters being very hard to
convince of the necessity for either reduction in
hours, or increase of pay. And it was the general
opinion the controversy would have to be decided
by appealing to the umpire, however this
alternative was avoided by the manner in which
the employers laid themselves open to conviction,
for after much discussion, the masters offered to
allow the deduction of the time asked for, viz.,
21 hours per week, cud an advance in wages of
Is. per week in lieu of is. the original demand.
This was unanimously accepted on the part of the
men, and will come into operation on the it of
May.

DUDLEY.
lIE CARPENTERS AND JOINERS.

At a meeting of the Carpenters and joiners, held
at Dudley, in the early part of the year, it was re-
solved that a memorial should be forwarded to the
employers, requesting them to increase the men's
wages to 1 is. per week, and also to reduce the
hours of labour from 581 hours* to 54, Last

week, the employers sent a replY, 'stating that at
present they were unable to advance the men's
wages, and that if a reduction was made in the
hours of labour a corresponding reduction in the
wages would follow. A meeting of the trade was
called on Saturday night, and after a deal of
discussion it was resolyed :—" That we, the car-
penters and joiners of Dudley, consider the reply
of our employers very unsatisfactory, and we
hereby decide that unless our .demands are con-
ceded we shall cease work on Saturday next."
The men expressed their willingness to meet the
masters and discuss the points in dispute, or to
have the whole question re&rred to some arbitra-
tor. The meeting was unanimous throughout.

LYNN.
THE BUILDING TRADE.

A meeting of workmen employed in the build-
ing trades in Lynn was held on Thursday even
-
mg, at the Bowling-green, Checker-street, Mr.
George Anderson presiding, to receive the decision
of the masters relative to the reduction of hours.
The Chairman' in opening the proceedings, re-
marked with reference to the object for which
they had met that evening, it would be remembered
that a similar meeting to the present was held a
fortnight since, at which a committee of workmen
was elected to wait upon the masters, and ask
them to reduce the hours of labour from 58 to 54
hours per week, and to allow the present rate of
wages to be continued. The committee had
accordingly waited upon the masters, and Messrs
Brown, Bardell Brothers, and Bennett had readily

agreed to meet the comraitte by reducing the hours
to 56} per week, and had promised that there
should be no reduction in the rate of wages.
The committee had decided to accept this arrange-
ment, and he hoped it would be agreeable to the
meeting. The terms were unanimously accepted.

articles.title: MAIDSTONE. MOVEMENT OF CARPENTERS.
articles.text:
MAIDSTONE.
MOVEMENT OF CARPENTERS.

An agitation has been carrried on hero for some
menthe past for the nine hours' movement; and
ik lot of correspondence has passed between the
employers and the employed. The men at first
asked for 7d. per hour and flfty-four hours to.
constitute a week's work, and the employers
flatly refused to give them any one thing, either
the code of working rules or the 7d. per hour;
and they asked them to receive a deputation
which they did, and after the conference they
agreed to give 6id. per hour, and throw the
code of working rules out of the question-56i
hours to be a week's work for summer, and 60i
for winter. The men carefully considered the
same, and offerred to take 6id. per hour for
54 hours in summer, and 50i in winter, and with-
draw to rules all but the arbitration clause, and
amended the overtime clause to this shape-Bd.
per hour for the first two hours, and time and a
half until the next morning. The employers
decided that they would not alter their decision;
and at a meeting held on Monday morning of
carpenters only, it was decided that they would not
go to work on the present offer made by the
employers, but adhere to their resolution of Mon-
day last; and consequently they turned out to
the number of about 70.

articles.title: STAFFORDSHIRE.
articles.text:
STAFFORDSHIRE.

Tax warms.

On Wednesday night a large meeting of miners
was held at West Bromwich m support of the
Government bill for the payment of wages. The
present system of payment was condemned, the
speakers characterising it as in many eases the
worst form of "truck." Mr. Baugh presided.
Mr. Capper (Briefly Hill), moved the following
resolution :
" That this meeting beg!‘ to thank her Majesty's
Government for having introduced a bill which
makes the payment of wages weekly .without de-
ductions, and further expresses a hope that the
Government *ill press the measure through both
Houses of Parliament to make it become law that
the wages of all working men be paid weekly,
without any deductions whatever; and that this
meeting repudiates the statement so industriously
circulated that the working men of this country
have no interest in the weekly payment of wages
without deductions."
Mr. Brand seconded the resolution, which was
supported by Mr. Alex Macdonald, and carried.
Mr. Cox moved the second resolution, calliog on
the borough members to give their assistance and
support in carrying the Government measure.
Mr. Randall (West Bromwich), seconded the
resolution.

----- -
Mr. Kane, Secretary
.to the North of England
Ironworks Association, supported the resolution,
which was unanimously carried.
• A committee of five was elected with power to
add to their number for the purpose of correspond-
ing with the memb-ers /or the county and borough
on the subject, and forming a representation of
labour association for that district.
The meeting terminated with a vote of thanks to
the Chairman.

THE AGRICULTURAL

LABOURERS.

WARW ICKSIIIRE.-At a meeting of the Warwick-
shire Chamber of Agriculture on Saturday a
resolution was adopted in favour of the bill
regulating the employment of children in agricul-
ture. It was then moved by Lord Denbigh, and
seconded by Mr. Muutz, that the secretary be
instructed to acknowledge the letter of the secretary

of the Agricultural Labourers' Union, dated April
29, postponing the preliminary conference, and to
further explain that the chairman and two other
members of the chamber will be willing to meet

any three persons appointed by the committee of
the Agricultural Labourers' Union as their repre-
sentatives. The resolution was unanimously

adopted, The speeches were conciliatory, and
expressed a strong desire to settle the question on
an equitable basis.
On Wednesday the Executive Committee of the
Warwickshire Labourers' Union met at Leaming-
ton, for the transaction of business. A letter was

read from Mr. Suffolk, Secretary of the Warwick-
shire Chamber of Agriculture, renewing the offer

previously made by the Chamber for the confer-
ence between the representatives of the Chamber
and the Union, with the view of settling the

_ •
existing differences. A fortnight ago the committee
declined the offer because the Union was not

sufficiently organised, but the committee on
Wednesday decided to appoint Messrs. Arch,
Haynes, and Arnold to meet three representatives i
of the Chamber to arrange preliminaries for the
proposed conference. The committee made ar-
rangements for promoting the National Labourers'
Conference proposed to be held at Leamington,
and thanked the public for the liberal feelings
evinced in suppOrting the movement.
DEVONSKIRE.—The labourers' strike in South
Hams, the richest agricultural district in Devon-
shire, which was to have taken effect has been
averted for the present through the acceptance by
the men of the farmers' offer of 12s. weekly with
present privileges. The settlement is jeopardised,
however, by the farmers having singled out a few
loaders of the movement, and unanimously refused
to give them employment. A union is to be
formed shortly, when other demands will be pre-
ferred. _ _ .

----
BERKBIIIitE.—In several parts of this county
farmers have voluntarily increased the wages of
their labourers. A few days since there was a
large gathering of carters and others employed
by the agriculturalists at Lamborne, Shefford,
Eastbury, and East Gersten—populous villages
in West Barks—and the wages question was
discussed at considerable length, but the meeting
broke up without any definite result.
WILTBIIIRIL—A numerously-attended meeting
of agricultural labourers was held at Wootton
Bassett last week, no less than GOO farm servants
being present. Mr. Morris, of Swindon, occupied
the chair, and Mr. T. Strange, secretary of the
Warwickshire Agricultural Labourers' Union,
attended and addressed the assemblage, promising
the men that if they did not obtain the advance
they asked for, he would secure them situations
in the North of England at from 18s. to 255. per
week. It was unanimously resolved to form a
branch of the Warwickshire Union, and the local
officers were at once appointed.
DORBETSIIIRE.—A strike among the Dorset
hands lies at last taken place, but the agitation is
at present restricted to a remote part of the
county. The labourers of Milborne St. Andrew,
where, including all perquisites, wages averaged
120. 4d. per week, demanded is. extra, but the
farmers resisted the demand, and hence the strike.
The standing wages are Os., the remaining 3s. 4d.
being made up of overtime at turnip-hoeing, har-
vesting, rabbiting, Sze., of cottage rent, and the
advantage of purchasing wheat at Ge. per bushel.
LEIOESTERSIIIRE.—A crowded meeting of dele-
gates from the various agricultrral labourers'
unions in Leieeetershire was held at Leicester on
Saturday night. Addresses were delivered by Mr.
Strange, a representative of the 'Warwickshire
labourers, and by several labourers of Leicester-
shire itself, who entered into details as to the
mode in which they were compelled to live on
from fourteen to fifteen shillings a week. It was

SATURDAY, MAY 11, 1872.

THE PRESS AND THE AGRICULTURAL
LABOURERS' CONFERENCE.

OUR readers are aware that a conference was
recently held in London in connection with
the strike in the agricultural districts.
At that conference, Canon GIRDLESIONE, a
clergyman, whose name has been for years
before the public in connection with the con-
dition of the agricultural labourers, was
present. Some eight or ten delegates from
the districts where the strikes are going on
were also present. To these may be added
many members of Parliament, for the most
part men acknowledged to be active and
intelligent members of our legislative assembly.
And side by side with these a number of the
leading men connected with trades unionism,
as well as others who are known to take an
active interest in working men's questions.
Altogether the assembly was very interesting,
not simply because it was held in reference to
one of the most exciting and important move-
ments that ever took place: in England, but
also because a number of the labourers
were personally present and addressed those
assembled on the various topics that came
under discussion with a fervency and force,
and at the same time with a moderation of
temper quite remarkable.

We do not wish to exaggerate the importance
of this gathering in any way whatever, or in the
slightest degree to clothe it with attributes
not fairly and obviously belonging to it. We
cannot, however, hide from ourselves that the
movement which gave birth to it is of the very
gravest character, socially and politically.
Combinations amongst our agricultural
labourers may be carried on peacefully and
wisely; but on the other hand, at any moment
tliey may burst forth in the fierceness of
revolutionary tumult. The demand for
advanced wages may peaceably and tempe-
rately fit itself to the requirements of social
j ustice, and to the convenience of those who
own land and employ labour. Or under the
excitement of class stupidity and selfishness it
may blindly struggle for what may be ruinous
in its injustice towards others. We predict
nothing. We take neither the optimist nor
the pessimist view of the matter. We only
say that troubled waters aro rising which may
be usefully and even profitably confined within
bounds till they silently subside, or they
may break away from control and carry
devastation and ruin along with them.

In such a state of things there ought to be
food for thought, oven of the most serious
kind, for our politicians; ground of uneasi-
ness for patriotic men who are anxious for the
welfare of their country; cause for active advice
and help to those who have made a special
study of the questions raised by these agricul-
tural combinations and strikes ; whilst our
newspapers and our "able editors," by elabo-
rate investigation of the labourers' condition,
aud thoughtful suggestion in regard thereto,
ought to give their best thought to the settle-
ment of a- question which whilst it remains
unsettled jeopardises the best and dearest
interests of the nation.

Naturally, therefore, it was to be expected
that this conference would have given rise to
much speculation in the leading columns of
our newspaper press. That in all its phases
this pressing question would have been ex-
amined and its direct and remote issues
pointed out. It is the duty of a newspaper
editor to be acquainted with everything past,
present, and future, from the obscure question
as to the first man who scratched his head,
down to the winner of the next great plate or
cup. And yet, notwithstanding the public
interest in the labourers' strike, and in all else
that belongs to it, not one of our London
leading papers considered it worth a line in
their leading columns. Day after day passed
and yet no word, no thought, no caution, no
direction, no advice, no praise of anybody, no
abuse of even sturdy trades unionists. The
subject was simply not worth a thought. The
labourers belong to the lowest strata of wage re-
ceivers. They wear smock frocks andhob-nailed
boots, and live in cottage frequently not wind

or water-proof. They are not picturesque in
their reality; they only become so under the
artistic touch of "our special correspondent."
Why, therefore, should our newspaper editors ,
trouble themselves too much about them. if
they sought to go into such a question as this
they would no doubt find some necessity to
speak with reference to facts, and circum-
stances, and ideas which could be tested by
the experience of people interested in the
subject, and this would be dangerous ground.
It is much safer to speculate on the occult
meaning of political wire-pullers. On the
plots hatching between statesmen who see
everything by looking round corners; on
moral mysteries silently giving birth to
huge depravities On political an&
parliamentary tricks, interesting chiefly to
the ins and the outs in the House of Commons.
Still, some of our leading papers might have
said a word about the labourer, were it only
to tell him that others know better what is
good for him than he can possibly knew him-
self. To kick a man is sometimes better than
to take no notice of him, as by such an act his
existence is recognized. This much was not
due to the agricultural labourer. He was
simply unnoticed, like any other floating
nuisance which people wish away without
speaking about it, lest the senses of delicate
people should be offended. However, our
"bold peasantry" are not to be got rid of
thus, they are alive and kicking, and by and
bye will no doubt, without even "by your
leave," walk stoutly into the leading columns
of all our "Dailies," and perhaps even beyond
there, into the House of Commons.

articles.title: RAILWAY SERVICE GAZETTE"
articles.text:
THE RAILWAY SERVICE GAZETTE"

AND OURSELVES.

THE Railway Service Gazette seems to be
angry with us for publishing certain state-
ments Of Dr. BAXTER LANGLEY'S relative to
the proceedings of the "Amalgamated Society
of Railway Servants." luta the controversy
between Dr. LANGLEY and our contemporary
we have no disposition to enter. We know
how profitless all controversies are which are
not carried on for the vindication of principles
or the defence of honed and important in-
terests; and we know also how paltry and
how damaging to a good cause all wordy con-
tentions of a contracted and personal character
must be.

For ourselves, we can say that we have no
quarrel with our contemporary, and we wish
to have none; nor arc we at all thin.skinned
as to what may be said about us in the way of
direct charge or covert inuendo. If our action
in favour of working men's movements did not
rest on a solid foundation of faith and duty, it
would havo ceased or slackened long ago. But.,
we feel now, as we felt at first, that the cause
of labour is in reality and in truth a high and
a holy cause; and we believe at this moment,
as we did when we took it up, that to lighten
the load of the worker whose strength is over-
taxed, to increase the comforts of those whose
lives are made painful by constant drudgery,
to add to the income, and, therefore, to the
happiness of poor men's homes, and to do this
in a spirit of peace and with a view to the
interests of all concerned, is a good work from
which a man should not slightly turn back
once he had put his hand to it.

We stand now at a most critical point in
the labour struggle. In our great manufac-
turing towns the fight for the nine hours and
higher wages has not yet been brought to a
close, though so far, in consequence of the
briskness of trade, it has been entirely suc-
cessful. The agricultural labourers have, for
the first time we may say, taken up an in-
telligible position, and they have done so with
a clearness of aim and a determination of
purpose promising the best results. There is
not only material, but there is clearly a strong
mental force in this strike of the agricultural
labourers. They are following with admirable
exactness the example set by the great unions
in the skilled trades, and are filling the new
half-formed body of unionists with the quiet,
patient, determined spirit of the old associa-
tions.

The men of the railways have also a great
work in hand. They have been oppressed
and ground down by a system of work over
which singly they have not the least possible
outrol- Amy= 9f wages, lgugth vf WoQk-

day hours, Sunday work, or whatever is, or
can be, an evil, they must put up with and
suffer from if out of union. But all these
may be altered by the power of well-vganised
'association. Under ordinary circumstances,
no men aro more powerless than railway
servants. They have little uninterrupted
time for communication with each other.
And if opposed by their employers, personal
sympathy or kindly consideration are not
likely to reach them through boards of
directors. There never was a body of men
whose success in any effort they may make to
improve their condition depended. so much on
organisation and united action, and who,
therefore, ought to be kept out of those dis-
putes which lead to personal contentions and
division. We are anxious to see railway
servants perfectly agreed as to the changes in
their system of work which may promise them
most good. We are desirous that to secure
these changes they should act with absolute
unity of purpose, without dividing councils
or counteracting and weakening influences,
and any word uttered anywhere that can
have the effect of producing weakness and
division, is so much taken from the strength
of the men and added to that of their em •
ployers.
• This is not a time for ill-natured contro-
versies, nor for delayed action. If railway
servants lag behind the general movement
they risk the success of what they are
aiming at. We do not object that
our contemporary's statement as to its repre-
sentative character should be all it is asserted
to be. This, however, should only make it
thankful for help wherever it may come from.
Not jealous of those who offer it, nor anxious
to lessen their influence by a depreciation of
their political opinions or conduct. We pre-
sume the men connected with our railways who
suffer from over-work or under-pay, will not
be too particular as to the colour or character
of the political ideas of those who take action
on their behalf. For ourselves, whilst we have
given our attention more particularly to the
social condition of the working men of Eng-
land, we have never concealed our political
predilections for Liberalism of the strongest
kind in the political action of the country.
Nothwithstanding this, however, we are as
anxious for the welfare of the most Con-
servative working man as we are for th at of
the extremest Radical. It would not be well
for the political future of the country
U we allowed our human sympathies to be
circumscribed or regulated by considerations
of party. And we trust that for the future our
contemporary will bear with more patience, and
view with larger tolerance the action of others,
Ewen in what it may consider its special sphere of
action. For ourselves, we can only say that
we are old in this warfare, and we hope that
with some of the experience of long continued
notion we have also acquired a little of the
patience which earnest continuous efforts
brings to those who believe in themselves and
their principles.

RELIGIOUS INSTRUCTION IN
SCHOOLS.

Mu religious difficulty of the education
question has 'been put clearly enough by Mr.
DALE, of Birmingham, in the order which he
moved and carried at the yearly meeting of
the Congregational Union. We observe in the
daily papers I? declaration signed by ministers
and laymen of different denominations to the
effect, that as strennous efforts are being made
to exclude the Bible by law from Public Ele-
mentary Schools, the undersigned (not con-
nected with any Established Church), believ-
ing that such exolueion would be a great
national evil, feel it to be their duty publicly
to record their disapproval thereof. Simul-
taneously with this appears a letter from Earl
RUSSELL, apoligising for his inability to be
present, as usual, at the yearly meeting of the
British and Foreign School Society. ti
remain," says the veteran friend to popular
education,
"faithful to the principles of the society. Per
many years I have contended for those princi-
ples against the partisans of secular teaching on
the one hand, and, on the other, against the
adherents of the rules of the National Society,
Which impose the obligation of learning the Cate-
chish on week days, and of attending the worship
Of the Established Church on Sundays. It has
APPOIVed thftt tiny sytitcmo eim,ing mud,

omitted religious instruction must be faulty and
inadequate. It likewise appears to me to be
necessary that the society should adhere, with the
most simple comment and explanations, to the
words of the Bible. I therefore trust that the
society will continue its labours, and that they
may be more and more successful. In various
ages of Christianity, doctors invested with the
authority derived from the Pope or placed in their
hands by the schools, have added to the Holy
Scriptures, and interpolated doctrines for which no
sufficient warrant could be found in the Bible.
The attempts to make such doctrines a part of the
education of these islands have of late years had
much influence on persons of authority, civil or
ecclesiastical. The Jesuits of Rome are endeavour-
ing to gain possession of the means of education in
Ireland, and the Jesuits of Oxford are working
hard to acquire control over the education of
England. Let us hope that these machinations
will be resisted by the lovers of religious liberty in
England and in Ireland. It is to be hoped that ,
next year the members of the Government will
declare themselves enemies to all oppression of
Dissenters; for they cannot expect a Baptist
parent will be satisfied to pay a tax for the pro-
motion of infant baptism, or that a Presbyterian
will be willing to send his son to church to pray
for a blessing on the order of bishops. These at-
tacks on freedom of conscience must be relin-
quished, and probably will be so before any long
time shall elapse. The state of Ireland in respect
of education is more critical. Unless speedily
checked by the House of Commons, the Ultramon-
tane party, which had so signal a triumph last year
at Rome, will next year gain a triumph equally
signal at Dublin. For my part I wilt only say
that this is not a time when either the liberal
clergy of the Establishment or the Protestant
Dissenters ought to go to sleep." The above
was written by his lordship's secretary, and the
noble earl, in his own handwriting he added,
"Let them be up and active."

Now, there is no opposition between these
sentiments and the foregoing declaration, and
the motion carried by Mr. DALE at the meeting
of the only body entitled and qualified to
speak the voice of his own large and important
denomination. The same remark holds good
as to the resolution carried at the meeting
which it has been so long the habit of Earl
RUSSELL to attend—namely :
"That this meeting, believing that the roa ding
and study of the Bible, without the 1180 of any
formularies, secures what is most important in the
religious teaching of the schools, both elementary
and normal, commends the plan of the British and
Foreign School Society to the friends of education
of all sects and parties as the most satisfactory
basis of union."

Mr. DALE'S successful motion is to the
following effect :—" That the Union desires
especially to thank the committee for its
action in relation to the educational policy of
the Government, and to express its hearty
concurrence with the great principle affirmed
by the Manchester Conference, that, in any
system of national education, secular instruc-
tion alone should be provided by the State,
the care of religious instruction being com-
mitted to the solicitude of parents and
churches."

Who, then, is attempting to " exclude the
Bible by law ? " Certainly not the Congrega-
tional Union. What its pronouncement on
the question desiderates is, not that religious
instruction should be omitted in the education
of the children of the people, but that it should
be omitted from the State provision made for
that purpose. The advocates of State churches
and those who claim to have the whole business
of education placed under the direction of the
clergy, are consistent enough in their demand
that the religious instruotion should be pro-
vided in the one case by the Government, and
in the other by the priesthood; but those who
object to State patronage and control in matters
of religion, and who hold that individual con-
sciences are amenable to God alone directly and
are in no way subject to human authority,
cannot consistently allow either civil adminis-
trations or sacerdotal inspirations to meddle
with the schools of the people in reference to
points of religious faith or practice, but are
bound to protest and. contend against either,
against both.
It is to be hoped that the warning words of
Earl RUSSELL will sink deep into the minds of
the English people. Were they to be the last
uttered by him, they would be a precious
legacy. Any verbal variance between him
and tho Society to which he refers on the
one hand, and Mr. DALE'S clear enunciation
on the other, is more apparent than real. The
schools on the British system are indubitably
unsectariart. From one you may learn them
all. Here it is lying before us, the names of
the committee and the names of the sub-
scribers; in both we find xneu of the following

articles.title: CONTAGIOUS DISEASES QUESTION.
articles.text:
THE CONTAGIOUS DISEASES QUES-
TION.

WE have the honour to receive and record
the views of correspondents as eminent in
character and in capacity .as those who com-
municate with the foremost of our con-
temporaries. Leaving them at full liberty to
propound their own sentiments in their own
way, we rarely interpose with observations of
ours on the subjects which they discuss.
Last week's paper, however, contains a short
letter, signed " which calls for some
remark. It relates to the Contagious Diseases
Acts, on the policy of which we have been
constrained by a sense of duty to avow opinions
not accordant with those indicated by the
learned writer. He was consulted, it appears,
by a married woman, to whom, if not to her
child also, the syphilitic virus had been con-
veyed by their own husband and father. The
facts are shocking, and no right-minded man
can think without loathing of so beastly and
worthless a fellow.

But, when our correspondent appeals to us,
saying "This is the state of things which some
well-meaning people wish to perpetuate," and
asking, " Pray, Sir, what has this truly
unfortunate woman done that the liberty of
prostitutes to infect men should be maintained
at her expense, and at that of the child at her
breast ?" When we say we are, on this
account, called upon to abandon our opposition
to the statutes in question, we cannot perceive
the sufficiency of the implied argument.
Granted, that the " clerk " who acted thus
basely did a foul injury to those whom ho had
given the highest claim to his most loving
regard ; still, if conjugal and paternal duty is
to be made matter of consideration, a wider
view must be taken than that which confines
itself to the physical injury inflicted, oven
though that injury be contemplated in its
effect upon future generations from the same
polluted stock.
Our " M.D." speaks of "the liberty of pros-

titutes to infect men." What does he mean
by the implication that he would take that
liberty away. Simply that he would take
infected prostitutes out of the streets, cleanse
them from the disease, and then set them free
to pursue the wretched calling they have come
to follow. What, in that case happens to the
man of whom his filthy " olerk " is "a type, and
of their wives and children? Precisely this :
they might, under such circumstances, con-
tinue to set at nought their conjugal vows and
their fatherly duties, with less fear of discovery
on the part of their wives and children. The
prostitutes would, it may be, lose their liberty
to infect men with physical disease, but they
would gain increased liberty to alienate them
from those so deeply wronged by such asso-
ciation.

We should shrink from underrating the
amount of a confessed evil, lest the conse-
quence might be a diminished zeal in
endeavouring to root it up. But it
may be questioned whether the extent and
the virulence of the pest in question are such
as to afford a sufficient plea for legislation like
that stealthily brought in. At what stage in
the history of the race, this obnoxious disease
first showed itself, there are no records to
show. At the close of the fifteenth century
however, it was brought to Europe by the
followers of COLUMBUS. Before the century
ended, it appeared in Scotland, between which
and the continent there was then more inter-
course than between England and France.
Curiously enough, King JAMES ordered all
infected, by it to be sent to the Isle of Inch-
kerth, "there to remain while GOD provided
for their health." It was at first believed by
many persons that the infection came by the
air without contact between the sexes. Hence,
0,0 Dr, WiaTILEALLUD idgma its, th 9 augtiol

praotioners of the time did not scruple
to publish the oases of princes, abbots, bishops,
cardinals, and even popes, who laboured under
the venereal disease. An edifying picture,
truly ! We refer to medical testimony, how-
ever, chiefly to moderate the fervour of those
professional gentlemen whom nothing will
content but such action as that taken under
the Contagious Diseases Acts. "During a
century," says a medical writer of high
attainments and considerable authority, "the
disease continued to rage with little abate-
ment; gradually, however, the complaint
became milder, and, at the present clay, had
lost, under judicious treatment, a great por-
tion of that virulent character by which it was
originally distinguished." This was said
thirty years ago; and, even in 1838, it was
shown by the REGISTRAR-GENERAL'S reports,
that only seventy-three persons (thirty men
and forty-three women) died of the complaint
in all England during a whole year.

articles.title: SCOTCH EDUCITION BILL.
articles.text:
THE SCOTCH EDUCITION BILL.

IF religious instruction in schools is any-
where a reality, it is so in Scotland. The
late LORD ADVOCATE, in his motion on
Monday night, founded himself upon the
practice of the past. When, however,
the subjeet is sorutinised, discovery is made
that king liNox, though a Presbyterian,
was as priestly in his notions of clerical
authority as if he had been a Roman Catholic.
He, like Cardinal CULLEN in Ireland, insisted
that the schools in Scotland should be under
the Church. The parish schoolmaster was to
teach religion, and the presbytery were to sae

him qualified for that office. Till within a few
years last past he could not act till he had
signed the profession of faith; and, even now,
he must set his hand to an engagement to
teach nothing opposed to Scripture or to what
they style the Shorter Catechism.
At present, however, he is under no
legal compulsion to give religious in-
struotion. The matter proceeds by confirmed
custom. As a fact, both the scriptures and
the catechism are taught. This, however, is
done at certain times and, no other; while those
ohildren whose parents may object retire from
the school-room. There are some cities and
towns and several country parts, in which
Roman Catholics, for instance, are bound to
meet this, and it may be, other oases, the
receiving of the religious instruction is made
perfectly optional.
Upon this use the Government Bill for
Scotland does. but slightly innovate. Only
the teachers are no longer to be selected, as
heretofore, from the Established Church ex-
clusively.
With respect to the houses of religious
instruction, it provides for that matter before
or after the other instruction on each day.
But it continues the permission to use in
teaching both the Shorter Catechism and
the Westminster Confession, not like the
Enlish Elementary Education Act, in-
terdioting the introduction of catechisms,
creeds, and other formularies. Against this
feature in the Bill, several leading

representatives of Scotland level notices of
motion which object to the employment of
sectarian standards in schools supported by
rates contributed from the whole community,
and would (one of them, at least) limit the
teaching to the Bible. This might satisfy the
people of Scotland speaking generally; but
will it satisfy the views of English Churchmen
whose votes enabled Mr. GORDON to carry his
superfluous motion? Leave religious instruc-
tion permissive, and, as present practice shows,
it will continue; but, unless it be made com-
pulsory on the other side, it will not adequately
serve the purposes of the BENTINOKS and the
HOPES On this.

THE BALLOT THROUGH THE HOUSE.
TUE Ballot has passed through Committee,
and it is well that it has. It has been clipped,
and out, and crippled in many ways—still it
is better than nothing. It has been said over
and over again that if the members in the
House voted by ballot, they would, without
hesitation, have thrown out the Bill.
This is perfectly true. It is the measure
above all others which the members of our
rich Parliament detest. There is an un-

many ,of them that they have no business to
be where they are. They 'know to what ex-
tent the old corrupt electioneering influences
have operated to get them there, and they
suspect that any system which destroys, or
even deadens these old influences, must be
detrimental to them. Every man who could
make any pretence by which to injure the
character of the Bill, did so. The ingenuity
of the members in this way was something won-
derful. The tricks resorted to were too trans-
parent to take in anybody—the chatter of the
speakers too foolish to be thought of without
shame. The Government understood the
situation and went into the fun in a spirit
suitable to the temper of the House. From
such an assembly the country had no tight to
expect a great deal, and much has not been
granted. Still we say it is better than noth-
ing. How it will work must remain for some
time a mystery. In the counties the first or
secon4 general elections may not show much
change. Fa rrao r' H questions, however, • will
follow, labourer's qnestions, and on these
questions -farmers are likely enough to have
wills of their own.

In the boroughs men of full purses but
seedy brains, may find things not quite so
pleasant. We have lying all around us un-
expressed thought on all sorts of tabooed
questions. Who suspeotedn few months since
that the farm labourers of England would
come together in their thousands with a cause
and a flag of their own. Parliamentary
candidates have hitherto shirked questions
to which the rich and. powerful had an
antipathy. Under the Ballot thp rich and
the powerful are likely enough to be
boiled out by quite uninfluential people, made
strong by the new power the ballot confers on
them. .

• That all sorts of schemes will be tried to
make the measure of no effect is certain; but
to what extent these will operate has yet to
be discovered. Patience and watchfulness
will be needed. by liberal men during the first
working of the ballot. But the groat duty of
its friends will be to educate public thought;
to interest the public) mind in the growth of
great principles; to secure votes for ideas,
for sound national policies, and not for land-
owners or fat manufacturers; who, so their
own purposes are served, care little about the
growth of popular freedom or happiness'in the
nation. Tho amenders of the Ballot Bill and
the squabbling debaters who tried to talk it
out of life, will for a little time yet no doubt,
taint the atmosphere of the House of COMTIIOIIO.
Many of them, however, will, when the
opportunity arrives, have to go—and in the
meantime—" An ounce of civit, good apothe-
cary."

The annual meeting of the above union was held

the resolution for adopting the report :—That the
union desires especially to thank the committee for
its action in relation to the educational policy of
the Government, and to express its hearty concur-
rence with the great principle affirmed by the
Manchester Conference, that in any system of
national education secular instruction alone should
be provided by the State, the care of religious
instruction being committed to the solicitude of
parents and churches." A gentleman in the body
of the chapel seconded the rider, which, after a
long discussion, was put from the chair and canied

articles.title: COAL AND IRONSTONE
articles.text:
THE COAL AND IRONSTONE

MINERS.

MONSTER MEETING OF COLLIERS AT MERTHYR.
On Thursday a mass meeting of miners took
place on the summit of the range of mountains
Which separate Merthyr from Aberdare. The
spot was judiciously selected, being at an equal
distance from tho principal localities whence
colliers and miners had tootravel. Most of the
collieries were at a standstill throughout the day.
The agitation amongst the colliers of South Wales
is for the purpose of obtaining an increase of from
ten to fifteen per cent. in the wages of the miners
connected with the ironworks.
A collier from Castle Pit, Cyfartbfa, was ap-
pointed as chairman, and discharged the duties
assigned to him in an intelligent manner.
After Mr. Henry Thomas, Mr. Isaac Kerniek
(agent for the. Merthyr district), Mr. Lewis
Morgan (of the Rhondda Valley), Mr. W. Picard,
Mr. W. Brown, and Mr. Thomas Halliday had ad-
dressed the meeting, the following resolutions
were passed :
"That, in the opinion of this meeting, the
wages of the miners in the steam coal
collieries and other mines and ironworks in South
Wales are not sufficient to provide for the needs
of themselves and their families but seeing that
the wages of the miners connected with the iron-
works are the standard by which other steam
coal collieries are regulated, this meeting is of
opinion that the miners connected with the iron-
works ought to seek an advance of 10 or 15 per
cent. rise in wages; and this meeting pledges
itself to aid the said miners to get such rise in
wages, as, by arrangements already made, other
miners will receive an equal advance; and this
meeting further considers the prosperous state of
trade warrants them in requesting such advance
of wages."
"That in the opinion of this meeting the Mines
Regulation Bill, brought into Parliament by her
Majesty's Government, is a satisfactory measure,
and begs to thank the Government forintroduc-
ing such measure, and expresses a hope that the
Government will net allow the Bill to be injured
in its passing through Parliament, and this meet-
ing pledges itself to assist the Government in
carlying the said raeasure into law,"
That this meeting highly approves of the
(Master and Servant) Payment of Wages Bill,
brought into Parliament by her Majesty's Govern-
ment, and begs to thank them for introducing the
said measure, and utters its protest against the
inutilation of the said Bill by the Select Committee
to whom it is referred. And this meeting ex-
presses an earnest hope that the Government will
see that the Bill is passed, making payment of
wages weekly compulsory, without permitting any
deduction therefrom 'or any purpose whatsoever,
and pledges itself to aid the' Government in carry-
ing their Bill into law."
That this meeting urgently requests the
borough and county members to support the
Government in carrying the Mines Bill and the
Payment of Wages (Master and Servant) Bill into
law.''
"That copies of the foregoing resolutions be
sent to the Prime Minister and the Rome
Secretary."
"That this meeting °Apnoea g hope that, the

Government will either repeal, or so amend the
Criminal Law Amendments Act, so as not to bear
so arbitrarily as at present on the trades unionists
of the country."
"That this meeting believes it is very desirable
that direct representation of our interests be made
in Parliament; and pledges itself to aid in obtain-
ing so desirable an object."

articles.title: IRONSTONE MINERS OF CLEVELAND.
articles.text:
THE IRONSTONE MINERS OF CLEVELAND.

As we stated last week, a great demonstration
of Cleveland ironstone miners was held in the
vicinity of, Saltburn-by-the-Sea, on Wednesday,
feE the purpose of raising their voices against what
they consider the coercive laws by which they
have so long been afflicted, and for seeking such
an advance of wages as would put them on on
equality With their fellow-labourers
,in other dis-
tricts. The day was beautifully fine and bright,
and miners from all parts of the district were pro-
ceeding betimes in the direction of Skelton, the
little village which bad been selected as the place
of assembly.
After the meeting had been addressed by Mr.
Alex. Macdonald in an exaustive speech, the
foUowing resolutions were carried non can. Mr.
Wm. Dixon, Bretton, moved:—
_

"That this meeting of the miners of the Cleve-
land district has with gratitude seen the efforts of
the Government to give to the country a good
mines bill. It is their earnest desire that the
Government will proceed with tho measure as soon
as possible to make it law, preserving in it all the
distinctive features of the measure--the restricting
of the hours of labour for the young, education,
weighing, not measuring or guaging, the constant
ventilation of all mines, the certifying of nil
managers, the daily registration of the state and
condition of all mines, and the inflicting of punish-
ments, without fines, in any• cases of glaring
neglect."
Mr. John Cunion, GuiEborough, seconded the
motion.

Mr. Andrew Norris, Brotton, proposed :
" That this meeting views with pleasure the
conduct of her Majesty's Government in bringing
Into the House of Commons the Payment of Wave
(Masters and Servants) Bill. It earnestly hopes
that the Government will press the measure through
both Houses of Parliament in its present form, the
payment of all wages weekly, and that without
any deductions for any purpose whatever.

Mr. William Coates, Saltburn, seconded.
Mr. Robert Spinks, Brotton, proposed.

"Whereas, we the miners of Cleveland, do
hereby agree this day, in public mee ting tlssembled
that, owing to our laborious and excessive hours of
toil, we deem it necessary to work only eight
hours per day; and also that deputations be ap-
pointed to wait upon their respective employers
to inform them of the same. (Hear, hear.) That
on and after May 19 we, shalt restrict our labour
to eight hours a day, commencing at six in the
morning, and leaving off work at two o'clock in
the afternoon, or as the case may be."
Mr. Thomas Matheram, Guisborough, seconded.
Mr. Jesse Wilson, Bretton, moved,
"Whereas we, the miners of Cleveland, have
for a series of years suffered much through the
defective ventilation in the Cleveland mines, and
the large numbers which are killed and lamed in
these mines every year is mainly owing to the
defective ventilation, and as our employers seem
no way ,desirous of improving the present system
of ventilating the Cleveland mines, we humbly
beseech Mr. MacDonald to use his best influence
with Mr. liundella, M.P., in asking him to make
known our grievances in the Commons House of
Parliament, and at the same time ask the Govern-
ment to appoint a Committee of inquiry to inquire
into the• condition of the Cleveland mines and
Mr: William Carter, Marske, seconded.

miners."

• Mr. John Ingledew, Skelton, proposed:—
"That we, the miners of Cleveland, do hereby
agree and petition Government to repeal the
Criminal Law Amendment Act, as we consider it
a one-sided piece of machinery, and one that is
likely to prove coercive and bad."
Mr. George 'Freeman, Brotton, seconded the

motion.
Mr. Wm. Coates, Saltburn, moved :
" That, owing to the high price of provisions
and other domestic articles which we are neces-
sarily compelled to secure for the sustenance of
our wives and families, we consider, as a united
body, that we shall not be unreasonable in asking
our employers for 2d. a ton on our present earn-
jugs; and also that we ask our employers to
consider the propriety of establishing a board of
arbitration and a council of conailiation—(hear,
hear, and applause)—as we are in full belief that
it is the only rational way of settling amicably
disputes between employer and employed, as we of
course should then rise and fall with the iron
market, a system of which would give us general
satisfaction; and also that the minors from the
various mines-be requested to appoint deputations
to wait upon their severkd employers, to see if they
will kindly grant our request."
Mr. David Elam, Bretton, seconded.
Mr. John Boulden moved, and Mr. Wm. Carter
seconded :
"'Whereas we, the miners of Cleveland at this
meeting, ao herdby agree to unite our best efforts
to procure a better education for the miners'
children. Therefore we wish to call the attention
of the Governlntha to the fact that there is
at this moment a large number of boys
employed in the Cleveland mines without any
restriction as to age, and that none of the boys are
sent to school from the mines who are between the
Ages a 10 And 12 years respectively."

articles.title: RAILWAY SERVANTS.
articles.text:
THE RAILWAY SERVANTS.

MEETING AT MANCHESTER.

A meeting of railway servants was held on
Sunday afternoon in the supper-room at the Free-
trade Hall, to promote the objects of their Amalga-
mated Society. Mr. R. Salmon, an engineman in
the employment of the Midland Company, pre-
sided, and there was an attendance numbering
between 300 and 400. _

The Chairman said an idea had got abroad
amongst some classes of railway servants that their
new Society was not being constituted upon a
sound basis, but this was quite a mistake. If
railway servants rallied round their good friend,
Mr. M. T. Bass, M.P., that gentleman would
continue his good services to them, and their
Society would soon be in a position to confer
much benefit upon its members. (Applause.)
A railway lurryman said the draymen had not
yet secured a fair day's pay for a fair day's work,
their hours being very long and their pay in same
cases rather inadequate, without the privileges of
other railway servants. The number of men bad
not been increased in proportion to the growing
traffic, and the consequence was that many of them
were overworked. So long as they had to work
10 and 18 hours, it was a mockery for corporations
to supply for their recreation parks, reading-
rooms, or libraries which they had no time to
enjoy without depriving themselves of necessary
sleep. Neither could they attend churches on
Sundays and keep wide awake or benefit by what

they heard.
A guard (Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincoln-
shire) said that many lodges connected with the
Association were already formed in Manchester
and neighbourhood. Their membership was
becoming numerous, and their prospect were ea-

couraging.
A Foreman (Midland) said the Society would be
in some measure a protection to the employers, as
none bt TIN cfidises of servants it embraced could
Ask 4or.,4L,cdncessions, and expect its support,
witho‘,lt ,sp,tiSfying the Society that their claims
were fair and just.
A Foreman (London and North-Western) said
he had just been relieved after having been at
work 16 hours. He often worked 72 hours a
week, and had tried a great many times to get
such long spells of duty reduced. The point, he
was told, was under the consideration of the Board
as it had been for along time, and he did not know
how long it would continue so, for the Board took
a terribly long vibilo to consider that sort of thing.
The continuant° of excessively long hours of rail-
way servants most materially affected the public,
for it was in consequence of the overworked and
weary state of these humble men that railway
accidents in many instances happened. In proof
of this it was significant that, since the concessions
handsomely made by the London and North,
Western Board in November, to the breaksmen
signalmen, and.others, there had been fewer acci-
dents than ever was the case before. (Applause.)
S. Graham, Derby, said that in the Midland
counties the Society was doing very well,:especially
in Birmingham. One disadvantage was that,they
had sometimes to work rather secretly. What they
wanted WAS a few independent men who were not
afraid of saying what they thought; but his own
rather mysterious discharge from railway service
about a month ago had rather discouraged some.
Several other speakers afterwards addressed the
meeting to the same effect; and at the close a vote
of thanks was passed to the chairman.

articles.title: LONDON TRADES COUNCIL.
articles.text:
THE LONDON TRADES COUNCIL.

We understand that a meeting of delegates
from the Trades' Sleieties has lately been held
at the "Bell," Old Bailey, for the purpose of
considering the propriety of re-organising the
London Trades Council, and placing it upon a
more satisfactory footing than before' both in
regard to its future labours and financial
position. Amongst the trades represented
were the engineers, ironfounders, carpenters,
bricklayers, bookbinders, carriers, bootmakers,
gasmeter makers, painters, shoemakers, cork-
cutters, stevedores, dock labourers' boot
closers, coopers, &0., &a. Mr. Wood, the
delegate from the ironfounders, occupied the
chair.

Mr. G. Odger, the secretary of the old
Trades Council, then read the circular con-
vening the meeting, and explained the causes
of the old council falling into abeyance. He
said he had received replies from the secre-
taries of several trades by whom circulars had
been sent, stating that the moieties had not
met since the reception of the circular, and
therefore were unable to appoint delegates
until the next meeting. All the replies
highly approve of the re-organisation of the
Council.
The Chairman said he knew it was the
opinion of all the large societies that the
Council should be re-organised. (Cheers.) A
good, and t3trong UKlos Counoil Wars iniPera-

tively required at the preaent time, for ques-
tions seriously affecting trade societies were
continually occurring which required the im-
mediate attention of the representative and
responsible body. An efficient council was
the only body that could effectually deal with
these questions. The obnoxious Criminal
Law Amendment Act, now engaging the
attention of the trades throughout the country,
would not have passed in its present shape had
there been a council in London representing
the London trades. (Cheers.)
The resignation of Mr. Odger, as Secretary,
was then accepted, with a vote of thanks for
his past services; and Mr. George Shipton
was then elected as the secretary pro tem.
The following delegates were then elected as
a provisional council, to act until the adjourned
meeting, when it was expected every trade in
the metropolis would be represented and the
council be regularly appointed, viz., Messrs.
Wood, ironfounders ; Odger, ladies' shoe-
maker ; Lucas engineer; King, bookbinder;
Coulson, bricklayer; Monteith, cooper; Matkin,
carpenter; Ratcliffe, bootmaker, Warren,
boot closer; and Harington, carver and gilder.
A deputation from the Nut and Bolt
Makers Society of Birmingham was then
introduced, and stated that they had been
locked out by their employers since the 1311
of January last to the number of 1,000 men,
for refusing to accept a list of prices offered
by the associated masters and gone on their
union. The deputation having satisfactorily
replied to several questions put to them, a
resolution was unanimously adopted, declaring
- that the nut and bolt makers of Birmingham
and the Midland Counties were deserving the
cordial support of the metropolitan trade
• •
societies.

CO-OPERA TIV E. EMIGRATION AND
COLONIZATION - COMPANY.
Ox the sth a May a leeture was-delivered
at the hall of the, above Society by F.
Wilson, Esq., on the sukjeet of "Co-operative
Villages." The lecturer laid down, among
others, the following as the basis upon which
alone any social community can prove a
success, viz.
That we have a clear definable notion of the
end we wish to attain.
That that notion shall be clearly and de&
nitely stated and expressed.
That the entire plan of action, or modus
operandi, shall be fully elaborated and per-
fected ideally before entering on practical
action; and that no awkward or crude attempts,
precipitate and undefined procedure, or shifting
expedients be on any account undertaken or
adopted.
That a most careful selection should be made
of suitable individuals for members of the
now Society—in a practical, intellectual, and
moral aspect—that, in fact, a superior system
can only be organized by superior men and
women.
That, being pre-eminently a co-operative as-
sociation, every member should be imperatively
required to work, and that the work of each
should be of a nature valuable in its essential
products or results—adding to the 00111111011-
wealth or weal of the whole Society.
That each member be appointed to, or
allowed to assume that function which be or
she has been by ntiture, habit, and culture best
suited to efficiently perform.
That the primary civil condition of the
whole undertaking will be the corporate
possession of the land—first and provisionally
by the Society, ultimately by the State—and
the abnegation of the present nefarious and
slave-producing system of " property " in the
soil.
