articles.title: WEEK'S NEWS.
articles.text:
THE WEEK'S NEWS.

in the supplement of the Nonconformist just
issued, containing a survey of the various
religious and educational societies that hold
their meetings during the present month, their
aggregate income is estimated at about one
million and a quarter sterling, of which the
foreign missionary societies absorb the greater
proportion.

The IVeBter-Zeitung has received a sheet
from Honolulu containing the German patriotic
song, "Die Wacht am Rheim," in the English
and Hawaiian languages. Between the two
versions there is a picture of the Emperor
William, accompanied by what appears to be
a biographical notice. The lower part of the
sheet is filled with the melody.

A few nights ago a man named Egan, and
his wife, when returning home from Clogheen,
were attacked and robbed, and beaten in a
most savage manner by two men. A portion
of Egan's head was found near the scene of the
outrage; and the injured man alledged that it
was torn from him in the struggle. Two men
are in custody who have been fully identified.

The West Cornwall magistrates, sitting at
Penzance, have for the third time fined a
father in gradually increasing penalties for not
sending his children to school. This third
time, however, it was proved that the child is
in regular attendance at a Nonconformist
school of its father's selection, but the prose -
cution urged that the Church school at Gulval
was the only one recognised by the School
Board, and therefore the parent was fined.
He, notwithstanding, expressed his uncon-
querable determination not to send. his chil-
dren to a Church school.

Shortly after two a.m. on the 3rd inst. a
horrible and fatal accident occurred at the
West Hartlepool Station of the North-Eastern
Railway. It appears that a shunting guard,
named John Egglestone, a single man, 25
years of age, was assisting to shunt a goods
train, near the Rolling Mills, and that after
uncoupling the engine he gave word for the
driver to reverse before coming out from
between the waggons ; hence he was caught
by the wheels et tho tender, and knocked
down on to the rails; his right log and one
arm being out off, and his body so frightfully
injured, that he died very soon afterwards.

Her Majesty, accompanied by the Empress
of Germany and her Court, left Windsor Castle
for Buokingham Palace on Monday, where the
Queen held a Drawing-room.

A brilliant assemblage gathered round the
President of the Royal Academy at Burlington
Rouse, to inaugurate the opening of the Exhi-
bition. Speeehes were made by the Duke of
Edinburgh, the Duke of Cambridge, Mr. Glad-
stone, the Archbishop of Canterbury, Professor
Tyndall, dm

His Royal Highness the Duke of Edin-
burgh presided at the annual meeting of the
Royal Naval Female School, when it was
stated that the expenditure exceeded the in-
come by £350, and an earnest appeal was
made for funds. •

Marshal Bazaine is not to be gratified by
having his request for a court-martial cited in
the order for holding it; neither will he have
the advantage of Maitre Allon's defence. The
order will purport to have been granted on the
recommendation of the committee of inquiry.
A Paris correspondent states that the bill for
constituting a special court will be introduced
at once, and that the trial will be held in the
Riding School, where the principal Communists
were condemned.

Occasion has been taken by the Duke
d'Audiffret-Pasquier, in presenting the report
of the committee on contracts, to inflame the
slumbering war passions of France. After
denouncing the unreadiness of the Imperial
intendance when the war broke out, and the
rapacity of the contractors into whose clutches
the Government fell, he eulogised the army as
a service in which nobler examples of patriot-
ism and probity would now have to be learned.
"Our children," he said "must all serve in
it." The Chamber applauded almost frantic-
ally, and resolved that his speech should be
printed for distribution in all the communes.

The superior Court of Cinoinnatti has decided
that an action will lie in favour of a married
woman against a third person for enticing
away and harbouring her husband. The
English case of "Lynch v. Knight "(9 H. L.
Cas• 677) was regarded as an authority on the
aide of the wife.

The question of civil service co-operation is
to be brought into great prominence at the
next general election, when the tradesmen
throughout the kingdom are to be called upon
by a London association to refuse their votes
to any candidate who will not support a hostile
movement against the Supply Asociation
Co-opmtiye 09Cieties.

Nothing escapes the vigilance of the Minis-
try of All the Talents, and so the Lords Com-
missioners of her Majesty's Treasury have re-
cently been exercising their great minds upon
the condition of the charwomen employed in
government offices. The result has been the
elaboration of a new code of rules and regula-
tions for the guidance of the ladies in question.

Mr. Butt has written to the Amnesty Asso-
ciation stating that, after mature considera-
tion, he will not bring forward any formal
motion in reference to Home Rule. He fur-
ther stated that he would accept the whole
responsibility of the movement.

The brig Etoile, of St Maio, 285 tons,
bound to Riga with a cargo of salt, went
ashore at ten o'clock on Saturday night, off
Chilton, Isle of Wight. The crew of eight
men were saved by the lifeboat Rescue, be-
longing to the National Lifeboat Institution.

The Mayor of Liverpool has succeeded in
effecting a reconciliation between the carters
of the town and their employers, and the
strike is at an end. The men resume work
forthwith, the masters having agreed to pay
295. per week standing wages,. overtime to be
at the rate of 6d. per hour.

The last of the pieces of sculpture represent-
ing the four, quarters of the globe has been
placed in position in the north-west pedestal
of the Albert Memorial, Hyde-park. The
group is "America," by J. Bell, R.A. The
magnificent sculpture on the memorial is now
nearly complete, and ready for uncovering.

On Friday an inquest was held at St.
George's Hospital respecting the death of
Riohard Major, aged 16, a groom in the em-
ployment of the Earl of Dunraven, who was
killed by being thrown from a trap near the
Grosvenor Hotel, the horse having bolted.
The jury returned a verdict of Accidental
Death.

We announce the death of the Marquis of
Camden, who was seized with a fit on the 2nd
inst., at his residence in Eaton-square, from
which he never rallied, but died about 8 o'clock
on the 4th inst. The deceased was the third
marquis, was born in 1840, and was educated
at Trinity College, Cambridge.

One of the bills presented to the grand jury
at the Old Bailey on Tuesday, was against
the Lord Advocate of Scotland, for the alleged
offence of withholding his assent to a prosecu-
tion sought to be undertaken against a person
living in the sister kingdom. The Deputy-
ReNrder ruled that even if there were any
offence oognisable to the law, and of the
character referred to, the case was not within
the jurisdiction of the Court. The bill was,
therefore, ignored.

A telegram from St. Sebastien states that
100 Carlists were killed and wounded- in the
recent encounter, and 750 taken 'prisoners.
According to a Madrid telegram, Don Carlos
has fled, with 200 followers, towards France,
closely followed by the troops. In Bayonne
the rumour ran on Sunday that he had been
captured, but that General Rada had escaped.

At the Central Criminal Court on Monday,
upon the application of Mr. Poland, on behalf
of the prosecution, the trial of Harry Benson,
who is charged with obtaining £l,OOO from
the late Lord Mayor, as the president of the
fund raised for the relief of the French at the
close of the late war, by false pretences, and
which has been standing over for a consider-
able period, was again postponed. The ground
for the application was that the prisoner was
still too ill, in consequence of the attempt to
destroy his life by setting fire to his clothes
while in Newgate, to be able to take his trial.

The tidal steamer Alexandre, Captain Paul,
experienced one of the roughest of squalls
whilst crossing from .Boulogne to Folkestone
on the evening of the 4th inst. According to
an eye-witness the boat, when mid-channel
about eight p.m., shipped a tremendous sea,
and immediately afterwards it was found that
a sailor named Alungo had been washed over-
board. His agonising cries were heard for a
short time, but on account of the rough
weather, no assistance could be rendered to
the unfortunate man, although the Alexandre
remained near the spot for about 40 minutes.
Poor Muugo leaves an old mother, whose only
support be was.

On Saturday an inquest was held in the
Board Room of Caraberwell Workhouse, on
the body of Herbert Edward Halfnaan, aged
38 years a labourer, who lived in Barlow-
street, 'Walworth. A. few days ago a young
man named Bankburst, a friend of the de-
ceased,
,committed suicide by leaping from
London-bridge, and he became very despond-
ing. On the night of Saturday week he
Suddenly disappeared from his home, and was
not afterwards seen again alive. On the
following Tuesday his body was found in the
Grand Surrey Canal at Camberwell. The
jury returned a verdict of Suicide while in a
§t4t4Q Vnout Mind, .

The Prince and Princess of Wales have, it
is understood, taken Totness Park, Sunning -
dale, for the Ascot week.

The unveiling of the statue to Mr. James
Ramsden, first Mayor of Barrow, will take
place on Whit Tuesday, when the Duke of
Devonshire will perform the ceremony. It is
expected that there will be a large number of
influential noblemen and gentlemen present,
upwards of 200 M.P.'s having been invited to
the banquet.

The Queen has appointed a Royal Commis-
sion to advise upon the best mode by which the
United Kingdom, its colonies and depend-
anoies may be represented at the International
Exhibition at Vienna, in 1873, aud that the
Pridoe of Wales, the British Ambassador at
Vienna, the Lord President of the Council,
Earl Cowper, Lord Henry Lennox, Lord Acton,
and Mr. Henry Arthur Brassey, have been
named commissioners, with Mr. Philip Can-
life Owen as secretary.

Four men, including a constalile in the
Metropolitan Police, were committed for trial
from the Southwark Police-court charged with
creating a riot and extinguishing the lights in
the Tower Subway.

The claim of the Earl of Aberdeen to the
Viscountey of Gordon, in the peerage of the
United Kingdom, has been again before the
House of Lords, when their lordships decided
to receive the documentary evidence which has
been brought forward in its support,

The Government has issued a notification
with reference to the Kooks executions. The
conduct of Mr. Cowan is condemned as unjus-
tifiable and inexcusabble, and he is dismissed
the public service. The Commissioner of
bal's, Mr. Forsyth, is also removed from his
post.

Messrs. William Blews and Sons, of Bir-
mingham, the contraetors, have received ad-
vice that the City of San Paulo, Brazil, was
lighted up with gas on the 31st of March, the
day of the Emperor's arrival at Rio, when 500
public lamps were handed over to the authori-
ties. The contractors have 300 more lamps to
erect. The price to be paid is £ll 14s. 10d.
yearly for each lamp, or I os. 9d. per thousand
feet, for nine-candle gas.

The Court of Common Pleas has made an
order calling upon the Tiehborno claimant to
show cause why all further proceedings should
not be stayed in the action which he has
brought to recover possession of the Doughty
estates, until he has paid the defendent's costs
in the suit of Tiohborne v. Lushington, and
give security for the payment of the defend-
ants' costs in the action against the Doughty
trustees.

In Spain the Carlists have received their
coup de grace. Don Carlos had got aoross the
frontier into Navarro on Thursday night, or
early on Friday. He at once took command
of the insurgents, and risked an engagement
with Morionas. It ended disastrously for him,
and he is now either a prisoner or a fugitive
Immediately on crossing the frontier he issued
two proclamations—one addressed to the
Spanish people, and the other to the army.
Like the Count of Chambord, he declared he
would never surrender his flag while a frag-
ment of it remained. Later telegrams from
Spain represent a certain danger of himself
and his banner have fallen into the hands of
the victorious General Morionas, The battle
is said to have centred on the village of Carasa,
which after resisting a nine hours' fussillade
was carried at the point of the bayonet.
The loyal troops made several hundred pri-
soners.

Father Hyacinthe's Old Catholic Committee
at Rome has framed a programme. It de-
mands ecclesiastical reform without secession,
and as a standard of doctrine it rejects the
decrees of the Vatican Council, but will sub..
mit to legitimate authority within the Church.

Denmark has taken the Irst overt step
against Internationalism, a meeting which Mt
to be held at Copenhagen on Sunday, connect°
with the society, having been prohibited. The
local president and treasurer -have since been
arrested.

Mr. Greeley's nomination for the presidency
has found partial favour with the New York
Herald, and is mildly apologised for by the
Tribune, but the Times ridicules it as a farce,
and the World regrets it as a proof that the
,Convention has been a failure. The platform
agreed upon at Cincinnati included an amnesty
and a thorough civil service reform. The
present state of the civil servants was solemnly
declared to be a scandal and a reproach to
free institutions.

Lieutenant Wallis loses two years seniority,
and Lieutenant Hailstone is placed at the
bottom of the list, while the other oflioers of
the watch are severely censured by the court-
martial which has been sitting at Malta in
refereve tc tliqftitrucling of thy, Lord Clycb.

The authors of the daring burglary, by
which upwards of £4,000 worth of scrip, in•,had
been taken from the deposit safe in the Vienna
Exchange in September last, have at last been
discovered. The gang is composed of men
with Jewish sounding names. They indili*
nantly disclaim any connection between them-
selves, but are committed for trial at an early
day, from which very curious disclosures ars
anticipated.

A terrific cyclone occurred at Madras on the
night of the Ist inst. The Hotspur, Armen/of
Burlington, John Scott, Robert SepPings,
Kingdom, Belgium, Invernesshire, Ardberg,
Duprey, and Delorme were completely wrecked.
The captain and crew of the Ardberg, with the
exception of six, were drowned. A portion of
the Hotspur's crew were also drowned. The
pier has again been breached, and great
damage done to the city and the suburb.

A case was before Lord Penzance on the 4th
inst., in which a woman who was a respondent
in a divorce suit, contended that she had been
led into evil solely through the means em-
ployed by an agent who was engaged by her
husband to watch her movements. His lord-
ship held the defence to be a good one and
decided that the husband was responsible for
the acts of his agent, although he might not
have given him specific instructions. The
petition was, therefore, dismissed.

On the 3rd inst., as several men were
engaged in excavating at Torquay Gas Works,
20 tons of earth slipped and buried five or
six. Four of them—kelly, Farley, Carpenter,
and Rowley—were removed to Torquay In-
firmary, where Carpenter and Farley each had
a leg amputated. Rowley, who had both legs
dislocated besides being internally injured,
lies in a dangerous state, and is not expected
to recover. Kelly had a compound fracture of
the leg; the others were only slightly hurt.

Dr. James Lumsden Brown, of Malvern ,
Wells, whilst walking on the lino of railway
at Great Malvern, was overtaken and knocked
down by a luggage train, the wheels of the
trucks literally cutting his body in two. The
luggage train was not proceeding rapidly at
the time the accident happened. The body
was removed to the Imperial Hotel, where a
coroner's inquest was held. The guard of the
train saw deceased on the line, but had not
the power to stop the train, or prevent the
melancholy occurrence.

A deputation of ssienee teachers waited on.
Mr. Forster on SatuFday, and laid before him
a statement of alleged grievances in connection
with the payments by results, and the mode
of examination adopted by the Education
Department. The right hon. gentleman, in
reply, held out no hope that the Legislature
would make any change in the scale of re-
muneration. If the examinations had been
stringent and capricious, it was contrary to
tho wish of the Department, and the repre-
sentation which had been made should be
fully and carefully considered.

On the 3rd inst. Mr. Edwin James delivered
another lecture on America, in Bt. George's
Hall. There was not a large attendance.

On the 3rd inst., at Shallee, near Nenagh,
in North Tipperary, a boy named Deligny, six
years of age, was killed by a neighbour's son,
also a mere child, splitting his head open with
a stone.

The Court of Common Couneil, though not
without a protest by some • members on the
ground of the extravagance of the estimate,
have voted £16,855 for the fittings and furni-
ture of the new library at the Guildhall.

A sale of water-colour drawings brought to
a conclusion the sixth and last day of the
great Gillot collection at Messrs. Christie and
Manson's. This day's sale realised 30,000
guineas, making the gross amount obtained
for the collection nearly 180,000 guineas.

Lord Shaftesbury presided over the annual
meeting of the Rigged School Union, which'
was held at Exeter Hall on Tuesday night.
There are now more than 250 schools, accom-
modating over 50,000 children, connected
with this organisation.

The Congregational Union, at its annual meet-
ing on Tuesday, adopted a motion, proposed by
the Rev. R. W. Dale, expressing hearty con-
currence with the principle affirmed by the
Manchester Conference—that in any 83reteui
of national education secular instruction alone
should be provided by the State.

Sir Edward Watkin, chairman of the Man-
chester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire, aad
South Eastern Railways, was examined before
the Amalgamation Committee on Tuesday.
While deeming amalgamation almost a neces-
sity in the present state of the railway system,
he thought that any arrangement wniob
tended to destroy competition would be an
unmitigated evil to the public) and an injury
to;s th 9 sualler compani9B.

Waterford harbour is to be made a harbour
of refuge and port of call under the auspices
of the Board of Trade. With this object in
view £BO,OOO is to be spent on the removal of
the bar.

Another step has been taken toward stamp-
ing out the latest insurrection in Merioo.
The insurgents have been obliged to raise the
siege of Matamoras, and to assume the defen-
sive.

In the Vim-Chancellor's Court an application
was made to remove the official liquidators of
the British Nation Assurance Association, and
to substitute in their place one or more of the
liquidators of the European, with which office
the association had been amalgamated. Vice-
Chancellor Matins said that, after bestowing
much thought on the matter, he had decided
that each estate should have its own liquida-
tors; but he had come to this decision solely
on the peculiar circumstances of the case, and
not so as to create a precedent for any other
"satellite 'companies," resolved on winding
up and appointing their own liquidatoro.

A Paris correspondent says that the speech
against the Empire delivered in the French
Assembly by Duo d'Audriffet Pasquier on
Saturday is regarded as the greatest ever made
in the present Parliament. The enthusiasm
about it is something astonishing, and it is not
only considered to have crushed the last hopes
of the Imperial party, but to be a promise of
concord between the legislative and executive
power. The Duke laid before the House, in a
compact form, the results of a Parliamentary
inquiry of fourteen months, conducted by
sixty delegates, who examined 1,800 docu-
ments, and he showed that France was robbed
under the Empire to an inconceivable extent.

The Marquis of Mindy has renewed for 19
years the leases of 37 of his tenants, three, and
in several eases more than three, years before
the expiry of their current leases.

The managing committee of the late
Channel Islands Exhibition, which was
held at the Island of Jersey in the months
of June and July last, have issued
their report, from which it appears that
during the three weeks it was open, 30,000
persons visited the exhibition, 10,000 of whom
entered on the first shilling day. The total
receipts from all sources was £2,518 17s. 6d.,
and the expenditure £1,983 10s. 3d. leaving a
balance in hand of £535 Is. 3d., which is to
be invested in the names of trustees, the
interest to be applied to providing an annual
prize for, or devoted to, any object calculated
to develop the resources of the island.

Prince Gortscbakoff's rtinionrect resignation
is contradicted by the Journal des Debats.

His Royal Highness Prince Arthur, K.G_,.
has graciously consented to preside at the 57th
anniversary dinner of the Royal Caledonian
Asylum,on Monday May 27, at the Freemasons'
Tavern.

Last week the Greek monks of Mount
Athos, who some months ago brought the
relic of the Virgin's girdle, the Titnia
Goa, to Constantinople, left for the monas-
tery of Vathopedi with their sacred charge
on board a Turkish steamer placed at
their disposal for the purpose by the Govern-
ment. The Titnia Zorn was borne to the place
of embarkation at 13aghtche-Capou by the
limit Athos monks, attended by a deputation
from the Greek Patriarchate, °misting of two
bishops and a number of minor ecidesiatics,
the procession being escorted by a troop of
mounted cavasses, and followed by a large
crowd of " orthodox " Greeks.

The Princess Louise presided at a meeting of
the ladies' committee of management held at
the South Kensington Museum on Saturday.
There were also present—Her Royal Highness
the Princess Mary of Teck, the Marchioness of
Ripon, the Countess of Warwick, the Countess
of Cork, the Countess Somers, the Lady
Dorothy Nevill, Lady Wyatt, Mrs. Fortnum,
Mrs. Gladstone, Mrs. Holford, Mrs. Alfred
Morison, Mrs. M'Callum, and the Secretary,
M‘Lcod of M'Leod.

On Tuesday the Empress of Germany paid
a visit to Columbia market, where her Imperial
Majesty was received by the Lord Mayor and
the Lady Mayoress.

Mr. Pennington's readings at Mr. Glad.
stone's residence in etalton-house-terrace
were on Tuesday attended by Princess Louise
and many other distinguished persons.

The new Board of Admiralty is gazetted.
It consists of Mr. Goschen, Sir S. C. Daores,
Admiral Tarleton, Admiral Beauchamp Sey-
mour, end the Earl of Camperdown.

.
In consequence of the inability of the South
Western Railway Company to carry more
than 2,500 men to Chobham on Whit-
Monday, the Volunteer field-day which it
Was propoaed then .to hold has been aban-
doned.

Early on Sunday morning, as the mail
steamer South of Ireland was leaving Milford
for Waterford, the internal tube of the super-
heater collapsed, filling the stoke-hole and
engine-room with steam. Five of the stokers
were badly scalded, one, named William
Welsh, so seriously that he died the same
afternoon. The engineer and others made
their escape from the engine-room. No blame
is attributed to any one.

At the conclusion of the debate in the House
of Commons on the Permissive Bill on Wed-
nesday afternoon, a conference of supporters of
the alliance was held at the office, 52, Parlia-
ment-street, when Mr. B. Whitworth, J.P.,
occupied the chair, and the following resolu-
tions were •unanimously adopted :.—Moved by
Mr. C. Thompson (Manchester), and seconded
by Mr. 0. Charlton (Newcastle)—" That this
conference presents its heartiest thanks to
Sir Wilfrid Lawson for re-introducing the
Permissive Prohibitory Liquor Bill, and the
members for supporting it in the debate on
Wednesday, and recommends that the earliest
convenient date be fixed for the adjourned
debate." Moved by Mr. A. M. Sullivan
(Dublin), and seconded by Mr. W. Lester
(Wrexham)—" That this conference congratu-
lates all friends of the movement on the proofs
of progress displayed in the proceedings on
Wednesday in the House of Commons; the
more numerous petitions in favour of the Bill;
the increased attendance of members desirous
of speaking and voting upon it; and the
testimonies borne on all hands that the
question had now become one of the greatest
magnitude and national urgency."

The Empress of Germany on Wednesday
visited the International Exhibition, and in
the afternoon accompanied the Queen to the
Royal Albert Hall. Their Majesties subse-
quently left London for Windsor Castle

Mr. Cardwell was on Wednesday waited
upon by a deputation, whose members urged
bun to carry out his original intention of
making Richmond a military depot centre.
The speakers expressed an opinion that the
soldiers would receive a hearty welcome from
the inhabitants of Richmond. The Secretary
for War intimated that full time would be
allowed for the consideration of this matter.
The right hon. gentleman also received, a
deputation from Hampstead, objecting to the
proposed establishment of a depOt in that
suburb.

The Victoria-park Preservation Society
having requested that her Majesty would be
graciously pleased to pay a visit to the park
during the present summer, Sir Thomas Bid-
dulph has been directed to send the following
reply, which is addressed to Lord G. Hamilton,
:—" My lord,—l have had the honour
of submitting to the Queen the address of
certain members of the Victoria-park Preserva-
tion Society which you enclosed to me,
praying on behalf of the society that her
Majesty would be pleased to visit that park,
and expressing their deep and earnest feeling
of attachment towards her person. I am
commanded to beg you to signify to the
members the Queen's appreciation of their kind
and loyal expressions, and to say that although
during the present season it may not be
possible for her Majesty to comply with their
request, the Queen hopes some day to have an
opportunity of seeing this great improvement
to the East-end of London."

His Gracie the Duke of Argyll will
preside on Saturday at the ninth annual
dinner of the Newspaper Press Fund,
which takes place at Willis's Rooms,
St. James's. Upwards of forty members of the
two Houses of Parliament and of the Corps
Diplortiatique have announced their intention
of being present. Sir Julius Benedict has
again undertaken the musical arrangements,
which have always been a special feature of
this gathering, and the artistes who have
volunteered their assistance will include dis-
tinguished members of her Majesty's Opera,
in addition to Mesdames Conneau, Urso, and
Carreno, with Mr. Trelawny Cobham and
Signor Caravoglia. As on previous occasions,
literature, Belem*, and art will be repre-
sented.

Marguerite Diblanc was on Wednesday
placed at the bar of the Old Bailey, charged
with the wilful murder of Madame Biel. She
pleaded not guilty. An affidavit was submit-
ted to the judge, sworn by the prisoner's
attorney, in which be stated that delay was
absolutely necessary for the purposes of the
defence. The case was accordingly postponed
to the June session.

A special telegram from Spain announces
that the Carlist rising there is decreasing.
760 insurgent prisoners have been sent to
Pamplona since the recent defeat. Don Carlos
has, it is believed, succeeded iu effecting his
escape.

A Bombay telegram brings the terrible news
that 1,000 lives are supposed to have been lost
by the recent floods in Vellore ; that 12,000
persons are homeless and 3,000 destitute.

The Mid-London Railway scheme was again.
before Mr. Hardcastle's Committee on Tues-
day, when several witnesses, including Mr.
Roger Eykyn, M.P., gave evidence in its
favour.

A correspondent at Naples, in some further
particulars which he sends of the.great erup-
tion of Vesuvius, says that the very shape of
the mountain has been changed, as though an
earthquake had taken place. Hills have ap-
peared where but a few days before stones
stood for visitors to rest upon; and precipices
have been formed which almost prevent
further advance. The path to the observatory
is covered with cinders a foot deep, and the
country round about is a scene of utter deso-
lation, not a single tree nor any trace of vege-
tation being left. It is said that two years
will hardly suffice to render the soil fit for
cultivation again.

A special telegram by Atlantic Cable from
New York states that Mr. Fish maintains that
the position of the United States Government
with regard to the indirect claims has been
misunderstood. No withdrawal of those claims
is intended; but the United States Government
will be pleased if they are rejected hy the
Geneva Arbitrators, should that rejection be
accepted as settling the question of neutral
responsibility. It therefore invites proposals
from Groat Britain. Mr. Fish has consulted

the Foreign Affairs Committees in both
Houses, and the general opinion Of the
members is in favour of abiding by the
original ease.

According to the New York Tribune, General
Butler intends to propose in the House of
Representatives that the United States Govern-
ment must abide by the ease it has laid before
the Geneva Arbitrators.

A telegram from Berlin anuounoes that
Prince Bismarck is unwell, but that no danger
is apprehended if be obtains the necessary
rest.

Further information from Spain represents
the recent defeat of tbe Carlists as so over-
whelming that Marshal Serrano believes there
will be no further resistance in Navarre. It
is said that General Morionas' force was less
than 2,000 men, while the strength of the in-
surgents is variously estimated at from 5,000
to 7,000 men. The Carlists were taken by
surprise, and the village they occupied was
carried at the point of the bayonet. According
to a Madrid telegram Don Carlos, on Tuesday,
was still flying towards the frontier.

From April Ist to 4th inst. the Exchequer
receipts amounted to £7,233,591, an increase
of nearly a million and a Twitter as compared
with the corresponding period of last year.
The expenditure has been £8,447,940. Oa
Saturday last the balance in the Bank of
England was .t 6,660,275.

Last week the aggregate mortality in
London and twenty other large towns in the
United Kingdom was at the rate of 23 deaths
annually to every 1,000 persons estimated to
be living. In the metropolis 2,340 births and
1,387 deaths were registered, the former
baying been 12, and the latter 117 below the
average. Sixty-two persons died from small-
pox, 64 from measles, 11 from scarlet fever, 6
from diptheria,Bl from whoopiug-cough,2o from
different forms of fever (of which 6 were certi-
fied as typhus, 10 as enterio or typhoid, and 5
as simple continued fever), and 9 from diar-
rhma. The mean temperature during the
week was 52.6, or 2.8 above the average for
the corresponding period in 50 years.

The funeral of Mr. Dasent, of Christ Church,
Oxford, who was drowned in Sandford Pool, took
place on the sth inst., when nearly 300 members
of the society and their friends followed the
popular young undergraduate to his grave.
The procession was headed by the under-
graduates and exhibitioners of the society
wearing surplices, and was followed by the
junior students, choristers, lay clerks, chaplains,
senior students, canons, and the dean, next to
whom came the coffin, with puce and white
pall, followed by the mourners and a large
number of friends. The service was read by
the dean in a very impressive manner, and
the body was interred in a brick vault in the
cathedral.

A deputation of rettil wineand beer traders
of the metropolis, accompanied by many
representatives .from the provinces, waited
upon Lord Kimberley on the 3rd inst , urging
several modifioations in the Lioensin; Bill
now before the House of Lords, The noble
earl admitted that some of the provisions of
the measure were open to amendment, and
promised attentively to consider the suggestions
which had been made.

Last week the total number of paupers in
the metropolitan district was 111,396, of whom
33,536 were in-door, and 77,860 out-door.
Compared with the corresponding week in
187 i, 1870, and 1869, these figures show a
decrease of 20,440, 30,907, 27,035 respectively.
The number of vagrants relieved was 833.

LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

FRIDAY.

The Bank of England directors, after a long
sitting, have raised the rate of discount from
4 per cent. to 5 per cent.
Ris Majesty the King of the Belgians and
suite, arrived at Windsor yesterday afternoon,
by special Great Western train. His Majesty
was met at the station by Colonel the Hon.
Dudley de Ros, and proceeded to the Castle in
one of the Queen's carriages. The King will
remain on a visit at the Castle, and to-day
will dine with the Baron von der Weyer, at
New Lodge.

Her Majesty will, its is unnerstood, leave
Windsor for Balmoral next Tuesday, about
which time her Imperial Majesty the Empress
of Germany will return to the Continent.
The Princess of Wales will not accompany.
the Prince of Wales on his approaching visit
to Great Yarmouth. It is understood that the
aocouchement'of her Royal Highness will take
place in June or July.
The Queen will hold a Council at Windsor
Castle to-day at three o'clock.
On the arrival of the last train on the South-
Eastern Railway at Margate on Wednesday
night, a stranger was noticed on the platform.
After the train was shunted his body was dis-
covered on the rails with his head severed
from the body. A bill was found on him
giving his name and address.
The London Rowing Club Four, in connec-
tion with the International Boat ;trice, is now
decided upon, and will consist of Messrs. John
13. Close, F. I. Gulston A. de L. Long, and W.
Stout; I. Le B. Smith being the spare man.
The crew went into training yesterday, and
will practice each evening.

The insurrection at Navarre is considered
at an end. In yesterday's sitting of Congress
the Minister of War stated that the Govern-
ment were in possession of very favourable
news, and that the victory of Oroquieta was
due to the plan of Marshal Serrano. A band
near Estella has been defeated, and aboat
3,500 Carlists have given in their submission
in Navarre. Satisfactory adviees have also
been received from other provinces.
The Manager of the South-Eastern Railway
has forwarded the following telegram, just
received from the Company's agent at Bou-
logne :—" Signatures suppressed. Passengers
now land without any formalities."

In the match played between the First
Eleven of the M.C.C. v. the next Twenty-
two, played at Lord's yesterday, the Eleven
wore put out for 99, and the Twenty-two had
lost four wickets for 18.

The Archdeacon of London (Bishop Claugh-
ton) will hold his first visitation of the clergy
of the arehdeaeonry on Tuesday next at St.
Sdpulobre's Church.
The Journal de Paris declares to be un-
founded the rumour of a projected marriage
between the Duke de Penthiivre and one of
the daughters of the Duke de Moutpensier.
A dreadful scene was witnessed in Chelsea

yesterday afternoon. Some children who
were playing with 'Lucifers set fire to the
premises of a dressmaker named Ball, in
Francis-street, College-street. The children,
William Niass, aged three years, and George
Niass, one year, were the sons of the lodger.
They were burned to death in the back room
on the first floor, as it was impossible to
rescue them.
The Courrier de France asserts that the
committee appointed to investigate the oapitu
Wiens during the late war resolved to recom-
mend the trial of Marshal Bazaine because ho
was responsible for the loss of an army of
150,000 men confided to him by France, be-
cause Metz was lost to France by his fault, and
because he failed to fulfil the laws of duty and
honour.
• The diplomatic correspondence between the
English and French Governments relative to
the Anglo-French treaty has been communi-
cated to the Assembly. It comprises among
other documents a note of the Minister, of
Finance, dated April 4th, 1872, in reply to a
despatch of Earl Granville of' the 25th March,
complaining of the vexatious proceedings of
the French Customs authorities.
A true bill having been found against George
andCeoilia Hurry,two of the "Peculiar People,"
they were on Wednesday indicted before
Mr. Justice Byles for misdemeanour in having
neglected to provide medical attendence for
one of their children, who had died from an
attack of small-pox. The jury found Hurry
guilty., and acquitted his wife. The male
defendent then stated that ho was perfectly
willing to act in oomplitinee with the law; and.
the Judge, in consideration of the high
character which had been given to the man,
ordered him to enter into his own recogni-
zances to come up for judgment if called upon
to do so.
In the Canadian Parliament a resolution
condemning the withdrawal by Great Britain
of the claims against the United States Govern-
ment on account of the Fenian raids luta been
rejected by a large majority. An amendment
was carried declaring it inexpedient to discuss
the question in the present state of the rela-
tions between Callada and this country.

THE TRADES UNION CONGRESS-
PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE.

IttPORT OF PROGRESS.
MASTER AND WORKMEN (CRIMINAL LAN,'
AMENDMENT) BILL.

Members of Congress, and other tradesunionists
who watch with any degree of interest and care,
the efforts of the Parliamentary Committee to get
the Criminal Law Amendment Act of last Session
repealed, or so far modified, that the injustice at
present inflicted on the great body of the trades
utionists shall no 'longer render them liable to
imprisonment for perfectly legal and justifiable
acts, will bo glad to know that there is every pro-
bability of such substantial amendment being
made as will relieve them of the inequalities at
present euftered by the members of our trades
uttions.

It will be remembered that your Committee,
after waiting on several very influential members
of the House of Commons and consulting with
them as to the best course to be adopted to effect
the object which the congress hadin view, prepared
a list of all the cases tried under the act, those
with a memorial setting forth our grievances were
presented to the Home Secretary, on March 21st,
by a deputation.
The very cordial manner with which we were
mot at the Home Office convinced us that the
Government would cheerfully do their best to re-
move any real and tangible grievance of which we
might have good reason to complain. Mr. Bruce pro-
Mised that careful cont3ideration should be given to
the whole of the eases brought before him, and also
to the special points complained of in the wording
and construction of the Act. Amongst those re-
printed was the Hammersmith ease, in which a
young man named Turk was sentenced to two
months' imprisonment with hard labour for distri-
buting bills giving informatioit in reference to the
strike. The decision of the magistrate was
appealed against, and, in consequence of the
nature of the offence and the severity of the
sentence, much interest was manifested in the case,
and great importance was attached to the hearing
of the appeal.
In consequence of your Committee forwarding
copies of the memorial, eases, and report of the
deputation to members of Parliament and others,
the whole question was very much discussed, and
some members expressed their willingness to in-
troduce a bill to amend the law, But this appeal
blocked the way, as every one said you cannot get
the House to listen to a debate on this question
until the appeal is heard and the question of law
settlod.

The appeal was fixed for Saturday, April 27
Meanwhile the Committee continued to wait upon
members of Parliament and others for the purpose
of supplying inforruttion, and to arrange the
details of the proposed now Bill.
The arrangement for this appeal case was not in
the hands of your Committee, hut we nevertheless
watched its progress with much care and anxiety.
On the day of the hearing we learned with deep
regret that the whole case had broken down by
the prosecutors withdrawing from the proseoution,
on the alleged ground that the men had now
resumed work, and they did not wish to press the
charge, and thereby continue the illfeeliug amongst
their workmen.
To this course the defendant consented, and the
conviction was quashed by consent, without, in
any way, calling in question the law as laid down
by the magistr ate.
At the time we deeply regretted this, inasmuch
as the question in dispute was the law as laid down
by the magistrate, in fact, his decision was appealed

against.
On the Monday your Committee waited upon Mr.
Vernon rfarcourt, and other gentlemen, and ex-
plained to them the whole difficulty of our ease, as
well as the delay caused by waiting for this
appeal, which had been frustrated without gichiev-

ing any useful purpose.
The costs, we understand, will be over £80; and
the young man suffered a portion of his imprison-

ment.
Mr. Vernon Harcourt consulted Mr. Henry
James, who was counsel for the, defendant, and
after full explanations had been given to the com-
mittee, as to the precise legal position of the case,
Mr. henry James cordially approved the object
and action of this coramittee,Eand promised every
help to get the law, which he strongly condemned,
amended.
It was then resolved that Ir. Vernon Harcourt
should giVe notice of a Bill at once, which he did,
and the Bill was read a first time on Wednesday.
Tho proposed Bill will. raped the whole of the
criminal clauses—that is, the first section and
oubeeutions, and re-enact such portions as are

measure. Mr. Vernon Harcourt, Mr. Henry
James, Mr. A. J. Mundella, Mr. Wm. Rathbone,
and Mr. George Melley, will be on the back of
the Bill. These gentlemen merit our sincere thanks
for the zeal and ability with which they have taken
up our cause, and the time and attention devoted
to the details of tie measure. By the next issue

PAYMENT OF WAGES (TRUCK) 13rTz.
Since this Bill was remitted to a select commit-
tee of the Home, we have been unceasing in our
efforts to secure weekly payments, without any
deductions. We have ascertained that the
Government tried very hard, and successfully, to
secure weekly payments. This we are told was
carried by a majority of ene only. But certain
deductions are to be permitted, the specialities of
which we have yet to learn. This we shall report
next week. During the time the Bill has been in
committee, most determined efforts have been
made by truck masters, and their agents, to
mutilate the Bill as much as possible. And some
two or three petitions have been obtained, under
what pressure we will not now.say, from workmen
in North Wales and Cornwall, in favour of "long
pays and deductions." These petitions have been
used unsparingly by certain persons for the purpose
of thwarting tho measure. It was the duty of
your committee to ascertain the facts, and to drag

have therefore had occasion to send a member of

Large mass meetings have been held in support

HOUSE OF COMMONS.-MONDkY.

EDUCATION IN SCOTLAND.
The main business of the evening was the
Scotch Education Bill, which stood. for Com-
mittee and, on the motion that tho Speaker
leave the chair,
Mr. Gordon moved a resolution declaring
that, having regard to past educational legida-
tion and the practice in Scotland, which pro-
vided for instruction in the Holy. Scriptures,
such law and practice should be oontined by
provisions in this Bill.
The Lord-Advocate, in objecting to the re-
solution declined to discuss its subject matter
until die House got into Committee. He
denied, however, that religious teaching had
ever been secured by any law, although he ad-
mitted that practice had always sanctioned it,
and the Bill would leave both law and practice
entirely untouched.
-Lord H. Scott supported the resolution,
and Mr. NPLaren also urged the necessity of
some legal provision in reference toe' eligtous
education, lest every parish in Scotland should
become a battle-field.
Sir J. Pakington complained of the refusal
of the Government to argue the point, and
warned them against flying in the face of the
unanimous feeling of the people of England
and Scotland in favour of religious instruc-
tion. _ _

Mr. Orr-Ewing denounced this portion of
the Bill as an indirect means of establishing
the secular system of education to which so
many members of the Government had declared
themselves favourable; and Mr. C. Dalrymple
also complained that it abridged and threw
difficulties in the way of religious 'education.
The, resolution was also supported on the same
grounds by Sir G. Montgomery, Sir J. Hay,
and Sir J. Elphinstono, who spoke of the Bill
as a godless and infidel measure, while Mr.
Bliley animadverted on the remarkable silence
of the Ministerialists. .
Mr. Eastwick, Mr. Wheelhouse, and Mr.
Seourfield also commented sarcastically on the
refusal of the Scotch Liberals to discuss the
Bill, while Mr. W. Egerton drew from the
Nonconformist Conference at Manchester, and
Mr. Powell from a letter of Mr. Winterbotham
to his constituents, the inference that the ex-
periment of Secular. Education having been
tried in Scotland, was to be extended to
England.
The debato was continued in the same one-
sided strain by Lord Garlies who warmly
supported the resolution; by Mr. G. Bentinek,
who referred to certain passages in the careers
of Mr. Gladstone Red Mr. Disraeli as illustra-
tions of what mistakes mere secular accom-
plishments might had to; by Mr. Hermon
and by Mr. Greene.
Mr. J. G. Talbot justified the course of the
Opposition in prolonging the debate so as to
prevent the point being decided by a snap-
division,' and Mr. T. Collins rallied the Liberals
on the unseemly spectacle" they presented.
The animus of the Bill was in the direction of
the Birmingham League, whereas all the
recent School Board elections and divisions in
the House this Session were in the directly
opposite sense.
Mr. Forster, who was received with sarcastic
cheers, said that if the Liberals had been silent
it was because they thought the point could
be better discussed. in Committee, and they
would not be parties to a waste of time. He
expressed his surprise at hearing the Bill called
a secular Bill, for it was framed on exactly the
same principles as the English Bill. It did
not interfere with the practice of religious
teaching, and indeed he would be no party to
the discouragement of religious teaching, but
it did not interfere to compel it by law, which
would do more harm than good.
Mr. Hardy protested against the attempt to
stifle discussion on this important .question of
.religious education, and maintained that Mr.
Gordon had a right to demand a debate. He
supported the resolution, because without it
the Bill would betaken to give a Parliamentary
sanction to secular education'.
Sir R. Anstruther justified the silence ob-
served by himself and his friends by their
determination not to be parties to what might
retard the progress or prevent the passing ef
the Bill.
After some observations from Mr. Newde -
gate and Lord J. Manners, the resolution was
carried against the' Government by a majority
of seven-216 to 209. The announcement of
the numbers was received by the Opposition
- with tremendous cheering. The Committee on
the Bill was fixed for next Monday.

THE PERMISSIVE BILL.

A large number of petitions, of which some
assumed almost gigantic proportions, were
presented in favour of the Permissive Prohibi-
tory Liquor Bill, the second reading of which
was moved by Sir W. Lawson. The hon
baronet went through the well-worn arguments
in favour of his Bill which have been so Often
heard in the House of Commons, dwelling at
length upon the evils of drunkenness and the
injury which was done to a neighbourhood by,
having public-houses forced upon it against the
wishes of the inhabitants.
Mr. Wheelhouse, who, in moving the rejec-
tion of the Bill urged the rights of individual
liberty, against legislative interference.
Mr. J. Goldsmid infused a certain clement
of liveliness into the debate by describing
some of the Parliamentary supporters of the
Bill as " itinerant lecturers," and the measure
itself as wretched, miserable, and tyrannical"
Mr. Melly's support of the Bill was founded
in great part upon its recognition of the prin-
ciple of local self-government.
Mr. Henley's opposition upon the fact that
it would throw public-houses into the hands
of reckless individuals who had no regard
either to their character or the proper conduct
of their business. The agitation in favour of
the measure the right honourable gentleman
characterised as most mischievous, because it
had banded together all those who were inte-
rested in the liquor traffic, and united with
them many who revolted at injustice, while at
the same time it had misled the public mind
as to the proper means of diminishing intem-
perance, which at the same timo he asserted
was steadily declining.
Mr. Plimsoll, himself a teetetaller, in oppo-
sing the Bill, told some good stories of the
inefficiency of the prohibitory liquor laws in
America—one which especially excited the
laughter of the House teferring to the sale of
corn whiskey under the title of Sacramental
Wine."
When Mr. Bruce came to speak for the
Government, he treated with avowed contempt
the oft-quoted statistics'as to the comparative
amount• of drunkenness in different towns,
and showed that during the period that it was
said that drunkenness had increased crime had
diminished. Prohibition, he maintained, was
impossible, and therefore he opposed the
second reading of the Bill; and at the same
time he contended that all the evils complained
of by the friends of the measure might be met
by the regulation of public-houses.
After Mr. Birley had supported, and Mr. H.
Vivian had opposed the Bill, Sir W. Lawson
replied, apparently with the intention of clos-
ing the discussion; but if this was his desire,
he did not succeed, because both Mr. W.
Fowler and Loid Bury spoke strongly against
the Bill, and at twenty-five minutes to six
o'clock Sir• F. Hoygate moved the adjourn-
ment of the debate, which was negatived by
a majority of 354-369 to 15. As, however,
the division was not over until after a quarter
to six, the Bill fell through. `

ACCIDENTS IN COAL MINES.

Mr. Dickinson, Her Majesty's Inspector of
Ines, has made a brief report to the Secretary
of St ate showing such a large diminution of loss
of life by accidents during the inspection of
coal mines as may well be regarded as proving
that the Acts of Parliament relating to this
matter have , been based upon a sound
principle. In the 10 years 1851-1860 the
number of separate fatal accidents in a year
averaged one for every 318 'persons employed;
in the 10 years 1861-1870 they averaged only
one to every. 388 persons employed. In the
first year of the whole series there was a
fatal accident to every 310, and in the last
year to eVery 423 persons employed. In the
10 years 1851-60 tho annual loss of life aver-
raged one to every 245 persons employed; in
the 10 years 1861-70 one to every 300 persons
employed. In 1851 one in every 219 lost his
life; in 1870 only one in every 354. The
number of persons employed in and about the
collieries is computed at 216,217 in 1851,
282,473 in 1861, 350,891 in 1870. The great
dimunition in the loss of life has been in
explosions and accidents in shafts, being those
over which the management has most control;
but the improvement has been great also in
respect of falls of roof and coal, in regard to
Which the miners have chiefly to take care of
themselves. The only increase has been.ba
miscellaneous accidents. This inc.rease, as
regards accidents on the surface, arises chiefly
from railway waggons; there having been a
great extension of railways ta collieries; and
also from machinery, there having been an
increased application of machinery for such
purposes as screening coals. The increase in
miscellaneous accidents below ground arises
chiefly from tub waggon, or trams, and blast-
ing, and is accounted for (1) by the transition
from sledges without wheels to tubs with
wheels, making the ' work much easier, but
more dangerous, and (2) to "the extraordinary
extent to which miners, to save labour, now
use powder instead of undermining and cutting
the coal with the pick, and then falling it
with the hammer and wedge." The increase,
however, under these heads is but a slight
drawback compared with the total improve-
ment; the " miscellaneous " increase is more
than balanced by the saving in shaft accidents
alone, in which the transition from skips and
oorves to cages and conductors has been, to a
great extent, simultaneous with that to tubs.
The w,hole less of life by colliery accidents in
the Whole 20 years amounted to 20,644. En
1851, the first year of the 20,984 of the
216,217 persons employed lost their lives; in
1870 only 991 of the 350,894 persons em-
ployed. Mr. Dickinson, referring to an alle-
gation circulated In South Wales, shows also
that in that district the number of -fatal tram
accidents to young boys has been rapidly
iiminishing; and really does not now seem
high, considering that the work in many

Wales district in the 10

It has been found necessary to introduce a
Bill into the French Assembly modifying the
articles of the Military Code which regulate
the trial by court-martial of Marshals of
France. The text of the measure which is
specially intended to meet the case of Marshal
Basaine has just been published. According
to the dodo, a court-martial called upon to try
a Marshal of France must be composed of four
Marshals and three Generals of Division; or
senior Admirals may be substituted for the
former. There are, however, not a sufficient
number of Marshals just now, even with the
addition of Admirals, to constitute a Court.
The Bill which has been introduced provides
that Generals of Division And Brigadier-
Generals shall be eligible. This measure will,
it is expected, be passed, no opposition being
